House again in committee on Bill (No. 88) to provide for the appointment of a Tar-riff Commission.
On section 3,

Has any action been taken with respect to the personnel of this commission? In one of the New Brunswick papers it was announced that a gentleman representing a New Brunswick constituency was to be appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The personnel of the commission has not been decided upon; it has not been under consideration.
Sir WILFRID LAUR1ER. Have the qualifications of the gentlemen who are to occupy these very important positions been considered, and what are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am convinced that the success of the commission will depend to a very large extent upon its personnel and that we need men of the highest qualifications. As to what the calling, profession or occupation of such men should be I am unable to say at present. The duties of the commission are set out in the Bill and while we have not decided upon the personnel I am of the opinion that we should have men of special aptitude for the duties so prescribed. The commissioners should be of high class ability because their duties will be quasi-judicial and administrative, they should be men of energy, ability and high standing. I cannot say further at the present time because we have not considered the personnel.

It goes without saying that the men to be entrusted with the duties contemplated by this Bill should be men of ability within their spheres. It would appear to me, however, that they are simply to be statisticians" simply to collect information, which we have already to some extent in some of our departments. Clause 4 of the Bill sets out that they are to make inquiry into:
(a) The price and cost of raw materials in Canada and elsewhere, and the cost of trans-

portation thereof from the place of production to the place of use or consumption;
(b)	the cost of production in Canada and
elsewhere;	-
(c)	the cost of transportation from the
place of production to the place of use or consumption, whether in Canada or elsewhere *	.
(d)	the cost, efficiency and conditions of labour in Canada and elsewhere:
(e)	the prices received by producers, manufacturers, wholesale dealers, retailers and other distributors in Canada and elsewhere;
(f)	all conditions and factors which affect
or enter into the cost of production and the price to the consumers in Canada;	....
(el generally, all the conditions affecting production, manufacture, cost and price in Canada as compared with other countries.
I repeat that some of this information is already in our statistics which are given to the public from year to year, and, m a larger measure such information is collected in the United States through their Labour Bureau or some such organization. I would say that the proper way to collect such information is by attaching statisticians to the Department of Trade and Commerce or the Department of Finance But it is intended to prepare a brief and to secure information for tne Minister _ of Finance in support of his own conception of what should be considered proper political economy. My hon. friend the other day, in the course of his observations on the second reading, told us he was a protectionist, a moderate protectionist as he qualified his own statement. He did not tell us nor have I read anywhere what is the difference between moderate protection and immoderate protection. I do not know that I ever heard of a protectionist who called himself an immoderate protectionist, he is always moderate. The line of demarcation between moderate and immoderate protection is a hazy one and rather difficult to define, it is like seeking the line between moderate drinking and immoderate drinking. My hon. friend will tell me that his ideas are in favour of moderate protection. For this I do not quarrel with him, these are his view6, but there are men in the country who do not believe in protection, who are in favour of absolute free trade and men who believe in a tariff for revenue only. Then there are_ men who call themselves moderate protectionists who are prepared to go any length in the direction. The object of this Bill is to collect information in order that the minister may find therein a support for his views of moderate protection. Perhaps my hon. friend will disclaim that idea and will tell me that the information collected under this Bill by whomever it may be collected will be uniform and will be for the advantage of ail.	.
There is another manner of collecting information. My hon. friend perhaps remem-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
bers what old Dr. Johnston said in his latter days. Speaking of the time when as a younger man, he was engaged in reporting he stated that his reports were always fair and accurate, but he always took good care that the weak dog got the worst of it. I believe that under this system the free trade dogs and the tariff-for-revenue dogs will also get the worst of this information. Let us have the information which is collected For all, for the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) who does not believe in moderate protection but who is a free trader as well as for those who are moderate protectionists, and even for the man who wants to have the barrier as high as Hainan's gallows.	_
We know now the character of the information that we are going to have. It is to be exactly of the character which I have stated, it will not be impartial information, but it will be information for an object. I may be asked what reason l have to speak as positively as I now speak. I have gathered my conviction from the debate of the other day, more particularly from the speech of the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) who, I regret to see, is not now in the House. The hon. member for St. Antoine spoke on this Bill as if he had been the power behind the throne. When my right hon. friend opposite (Mr. Borden) formed his Cabinet everybody expected that the hon. member for St. Antoine would be included in it. Everybody thought that both his exertions and the ability which he is known to possess in financial and business matters entitled him to a seat in that Cabinet. But although he is not a member of the government he seems to be the power behind the throne. He has proved that he has even more power in the government than those who are members of it, and, therefore, I attach a great deal of importance to the information which he has given us, and he has told us in so many words that the men who are to be appointed on this commission are to be in sympathy with the sentiment of the present administration. He stated that in his speech and repeated it in answer to my hon. friend for Carleton, New Brunswick. He said:
I beg your pardon, the words ' high protectionist"' were not used by me. I said they must be in sympathy with the well known sentiment of the present government.
Well, the well-known sentiment of the present government as defined the other day by the Minister of Finance (Mr. White), and vee knew it before, is in favour of moderate protection. Therefore, the men who are to be appointed on this commission are to be moderate protectionists, they are to be in sympathy with the sentiment now ruling the country. I ask my hon. friend opposite is it in accordance

with British institutions that this commission should be formed on such a basis as this? Is it in accordance with what we know of the continuity of government that partisans should be appointed in the Civil Service or on any commission? If you appoint a temporary commission the government may put on that commission any man they think will serve an object, but if you appoint a permanent commission such as this is intended to be, is it in accordance with the spirit of British institutions that you should appoint partisans, or if you wanted to put it less strongly than I do, men who would be in sympathy with the government of the day? This is absolutely repugnant to our system of constitutional government. The very nature of our institutions is based on party government, and contemplates that there should be an alternation of party in the administration. The very nature of our administration is predicated upon the fact which we know by the experience of British countries that governments are not immortal, governments are like men, born to die. Even this government is not eternal or immortal, there will come a day when it will give way to its opponents. If we appoint this commission composed of partisans, men intended to be in sympathy with the present policy of the government, what justice will it be when their opponents come into office? That is not in accordance with our principle. The principle upon which this commission must be governed is that the men who are appointed to it shall be absolutely free from any political bias.
If justice is to be done to the whole country, not only to supporters of the government but also to its opponents, you must appoint men who are not biased or partisan and who wTili give the information they collect without any colour at all so that every one may ascertain the facts as they are. They should ue men, not influenced by sympathy with the present government, but anxious to give the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The very manner in which it is proposed to appoint this commission justifies our opposition to it. I object to a commission entrusted with the collection of information on all subjects mentioned in the Bill which will do it with the view of preparing a brief for the minister and not simply for the purpose of collecting information, whether that information will help the views of my hon. friends or the contrary. I think the principle of the Bill is altogether wrong and that the method to be followed under it is not that on which my hon. friend should proceed. Complaint has been made that our statistics are not as perfect as they should be. I agree in this, but I submit that any legislation to improve our statistical records should not be enacted for a 91
political object, but simply for the obtaining of information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman is unduly alarmed. I am afraid he is not following out the principles he exhibited to the country during some fifteen years in which he held office. He objects to partisans being appointed on this commission. Well, nobody would select a man because he was a partisan, but on the other hand I do not suppose any one would reject any man, otherwise fit and suitable, because he had some political opinions. It would be difficult to find any one who is not affiliated with one or the other of the political parties. During the fifteen years during which my hon. friend was in power, when he appointed a great many commissions, I am not aware that ever, from first to last, he appointed a single Conservative to any one of them. Yet he informs us this afternoon that any such course is absolutely outrageous. How is it that this has occurred to him to-day for the first time and not on some previous occasion during his fifteen years in office? It is well known that in this country men who have taken very active part in political affairs are frequently appointed to positions on the bench, and we know that, with very occasional exceptions, they all, in spite of their political affiliations, administer justice as it should be administered. My right hon. friend suggests that if any one appointed on this commission should have any particular opinions regarding the trade policy of this country, that will affect his inquiry into the matters brought before him. The same objection might be urged to the trial by judge of a matter between two men, one of whom had been a strong supporter of his in politics and the other an opponent. Yet no one would venture the opinion that he was therefore not fitted to administer impartial justice between these two. I do not see the force of the right hon. gentleman's objections, nor do I think this is the proper time to consider the principle of the Bill, because we did that on the second reading and are now only concerned with its details. As my right hon. friend must understand, it would be impossible to name now the personnel of the commission. What we are endeavouring to do is to have legislation passed, and then we shall consider who are the most suitable persons to appoint. It would be reversing the usual order to decide on the personnel of the commission first and then bring in legislation for the purpose of establishing that commission and appointing them to office. The government will be responsible for appointing the best qualified persons as commissioners, should this Bill become law, and I have no doubt the selection will be one which will commend



itself to the judgment of all fair-minded people.

My right hon. friend (Mr. Borden) has -surely a short memory with regard to the appointments made by the late government, commissioners or otherwise, during the last fifteen years. Turning around to his followers and waving his bands he said that during the last fifteen years my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the late government never appointed on these commissions any but partisans. If my right hon. friend will reflect for -a moment, he will see that the statement was very inaccurate. If he will refer back to one of the important commissions appointed in the last four or five years, the Civil Service Commission, he will find that the chairman of that commission was, prior to his appointment, a Conservative of the most pronounced type. And if he will refer to the second Civil Service Commission, consisting of one man, Mr. Justice Cassels, he will find -that Mr. Justice Cassels, who was appointed by the late government judge of the Exchequer Court, was not, in his political career, on the Liberal side -at all events. I think I might recall other commissions of which the same may be said. In the appointment of the Civil Service Commission, care was taken that no one appointed could be -considered a partisan in iany sense of the word.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends laugh at that statement, but they know that Prof. Shortt was a non-partisan. I have frequently heard him speak, I have discussed party matters with him, and I can say that he was distinctly non-partisan at the time of -his -appointment. In the appointments of judges, the record of the late administration is anything but a record of partisan appointment, in Ontario, Quebec or Nova Scotia.
Name one in Manitoba.

Let me name one or more that I am familiar with. I recall the case of Mr. Justice Nesbitt, now Hon. Wallace Nesbitt, who retired from the Supreme Court. There was Mr. Justice Middleton, at present a judge of the High Court of Ontario. I think I am also right in saying there was the case of Judge Phippen, now connected with the Canadian Northern railway-a case in Manitoba, I believe. There was the case of Mr. Justice Townsend, appointed by the Conservative government and promoted to the chief justiceship of Nova Scotia.
And Chief Justice Barker of New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: And others could be named. In regard to judicial appointments or tlh-e appointment of commissioners whose powers were judicial, the late government did not seek the line of partisanship, but appointed, -as far as was in their power, men who were non-partisan,, men of independent judgment. The question, of course, becomes important in view of the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. White, Leeds), himself speaking on the motion for the second reading of the Bill, that various schools of thought in -regard to the tariff existed1 in this- country. He stated openly that there were high protectionists, moderate protectionists and free traders. Surely it is all-important for the members of this committee to know from which of these -classes- he will appoint the gentlemen who are to compose this commission. If we -had some reasonable assurance that there would be one from each class, I think it would be rather satisfactory at this juncture. In the United States, in their proposed measure, they certainly recognized this, for they provided for the appointment of five, of whom three were to be Republicans-leaving two to the Democrats or whatever the other parties might be. I think we should have some assurance of the personnel before the clause is passed. Perhaps, If the clause stood ' over my hon. friend (Mr. White, Leeds) might make up his mind on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friends opposite, I think, have not been earnest and sincere in their opposition to this Bill. This has not -been a real fight, but a sham fight, a pillow fight. That was quite apparent on the second reading. These gentlemen have simply been setting -up bogies and attacking them. They have been reading into the Bill what was never in the Bill, -and no one knows d-t better than fheon-selv-es. My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has assumed a good deal. Where is there a word in this Bill with regard to high protection, or reasonable protection, or free trade ?-or as to partisans being appointed commissioners? There is not a word; these hon. gentlemen have simply read this in the Bill for tlhe purpose of their own arguments. As I have said, the duties of these commissioners are quasijudicial -and administrative. I want men who are capable of getting the facts, of sifting out information -and presenting it in a form that we may r-ely upon. It will -be valuable to -us, as I have said, in framing a tariff. And it ill becomes Liberals to stand in the way of light and information. The consumers of this country want information.
We want the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We want the facts, and hon. gentlemen opposite are

standing in the way of the facts when they oppose the appointment of this commission. They are standing in the way of the light. The consumers of this country complain, as some of our free trade friends complain, that an undue measure of protection is enjoyed by certain interests. How can we tell whether these interests make unduly large profits, unless we get the information? And that information is not available at the present time. How are we to get at that information otherwise than is here proposed? Hon. members opposite talk about this as subverting the constitution. I think that argument is completely destroyed by looking at the case more in detail. Suppose we proposed here to appoint a commission to investigate one particular industry, let us say the cement industry, with the idea of finding out the cost of production and the prices at which the product is sold at various points in Canada, would hon. gentlemen opposite say that this would involve a subversion of the constitution? In the Customs Tariff Act, I think, it is provided that if there is evidence that a conspiracy or combination exists for the purpose of unduly enhancing prices, the government may appoint a judge to investigate and ascertain the facts. And vhat may the government do on the report of that judge? They may reduce the customs duty in order that the public may have fair-play in the matter. What essential difference is there between this and having an inquiry with regard to one particular industry and appointing a Tariff Commission for the purpose of investigating not one, but all industries, to ascertain the cost of production and the prices of commodities throughout the country? What is there prima facie wrong in that? Is it not commendable instead of being prima facie wrong? The only thing that can make it appear wrong is that hon. gentlemen opposite have read into it their own suspicions. They have approached this proposal in a suspicious manner, instead of in an open and a fair manner. As I have said, there is not a line in this Bill that suggests high protection or reasonable protection, or free trade. My hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) made some observations with regard to a statement of mine that I was not a high protectionist, but believed in a reasonable degree of protection, and he asked me what was a reasonable degree of protection? That is not an easy thing to define, but here is what I would say to my right hon. friend: If an industry which is capable of being maintained in this country, an industry in which we have some advantages and not such great disadvantages as to make it improper that 91i
this industry should be developed at all, and if this industry is capable of furnishing work to our labouring population and of giving reasonable profit to the men who are developing it, and if, by reason of a protective tariff an undue return is obtained by the men who are developing that industry, a return above what might be deemed an adequate and fair return, then I should say that industry was too highly protected. If on the other hand, we can build up industries in this country, if we can develop our resources by a tariff which does not permit undue profits to those engaged in that development, an industry which affords work to our people and produces here goods that otherwise would be produced abroad and imported into Canada, I think we may say that the protection that would have this result would be reasonable protection. And in saying that, I believe I am expressing a view which is not substantially different from that of my predecessor in the office of Minister of Finance. Read * Hansard ' and note carefully what he said, and you will find that the party for which he was the spokesman in tariff matters was not a free trade party, or even a tariff-for-revenue-only party. I think you will find any number of utterances on the part of my predecessor in favour of a policy of reasonable protection. This was subject, of course, to our having advantages for the development of industries in this country. I think he would assume-and I would say the same and would have no hesitation in giving adherence to this view-that there may be some things that we cannot manufacture to advantage, and, in the case of such industries, it mighty be fairly argued that there should be no' protective tariff.
Now, I have said that hon. gentlemen opposite are standing in the way of light and information in opposing the creation of this Tariff Commission. And let me say to them that I believe that if they had had a Tariff Commission to supply them with the facts, there would have been no election on the 21st of September last.
I state that it was because they were not possessed of the facts that they negotiated the reciprocity agreement with the United States-simply because they were not possessed of the facts and the United States was possessed of the facts by means of a tariff commission. My hon. friends opposite were not possessed of the facts, and the result is that we are here and you are there. My right hon. friend might have been sitting here to-day, and no election would have taken place, but instead of that, he is sitting over there, and I must say that he looks pretty well in either place, because he is a distinguished looking man.
Happy on either side.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: See that you are not on both sides. Now my hon. friend has spoken with regard, to these commissioners being mere statisticians. I must take issue with him; they are a good deal more than statisticians. He has read some of the subsections there which would indicate that statistics were to be accumulated, and I agree with him that as to certain of these subsections, statisticians might reasonably obtain information. But if he will look over them all carefully, he will find that very much higher qualifications are required in these men to disenarge their duties than the qualifications of mere statisticians. For example, the cost of production in Canada arid elsewhere-one of the most difficult things to ascertain, requires judicial qualifications, and other abilities of an unusual kind, because in the cost of production you find so many different factors and elements. In the first place, you have the cost of the raw material and the cost of laying it down. Then you have to consider how much capital is invested in that enterprise, and that may mean an investigation as to whether a company is over-capitalized or not. Then you have to find what are the fixed charges, the cost of management, and the efficiency of the management, because with poor management as distinguished from good management, your cost will be increased. You have to consider whether the capital invested was paid bona fide, that is, if it is watered, and to what extent it is "watered; in other words, judgment of a very rare kind is required for the investigation into the cost * of any commodity or product. In the same way the cost, the efficiency and the conditions of labour in Canada and elsewhere must be inquired into.
In deciding whether a ccmpany has been over-capitalized, will the minister require this commission to Teport the facts, or will he judge for himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will observe that in the reports that have been made, there is to be a copy of the evidence. Let me say this-because I do r,ot desire that there should be any misconception as to the scope of this Bill-I dc not say that because the commission makes a report that it is to be absolutely conclusive. As I said the other da

 the minister himself, must keep in touch with living conditions, he must see what is going on about him, as he does to-day, he must keep in touch with business conditions; and while this Tariff Commission will supplement the information he may have, at the same time he must use his own judgment, and if he has any Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
cause to suspect or to believe that the evidence furnished with the reports of the Tariff Commission is not accurate, of course he will re-commit such questions to the commission, to be taken up again for further consideration. As I remarked on the second reading, we do not desire to be relieved from responsibility with regard to the tariff, and all the Tariff Commission does, is to enable us to obtain information on which to act. Let me say this, that of all the people in Canada who desire information to he obtained, those who call themselves free traders, and the consumers, should be the most anxious to get it. If my hon. friends think they can score on that, I believe they are very much mistaken. I believe the consuming population of Canada are greatly interests ed in the question of the tariff, they want the facts and our protectionist friends, those who enjoy or think they enjoy a reasonable protection, want the facts also; in other words, it is in the interest of all the classes in Canada without exception, I do not care what their economic opinions may be, to have reliable information.

The minister says that he does not desire ministerial responsibility to cease. Suppose a couple of years hence the minister should ask the House to place a duty on certain articles and some of us should object; does the minister think that he would be justified in closing the matter by simply saying that the commission had found certain facts to exist? ,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would say this, that great weight should be attached to the reports of the Tariff Commission. But I am far from saying that they should be conclusive in the sense indicated by my hon. friend. I think the report of the Tariff Commission should be available to every member of this House as well as to the minister, and then no doubt it will carry great weight. But that is far from saying that it is absolutely conclusive.
It would not be a justification in itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not an absolute justification, no, but it will have its due weight.

I think this is a reason why we should know the personnel of this commission before this Act passes, because the minister argues that it is in the interest of the producers that this Tariff Commission be constituted. But it will not be in the interest of the consumers or the labouring classes if three high protectionists are placed on this commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Where does my hon. friend find in this Bill one word to

indicate that high protectionists are to be appointed commissioners? Not a word, he is finding it in his own imagination, and no where else.
We are simply asking for information as to the personnel of this commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can tell my hon. friend that the question of the personnel of the commission has not yet engaged our attention. Let me ask my hon. friend, did he ever know in this case of any legislation going through this House, of the personnel of the commission being announced in advance of the passing of the Bill creating the commission?
The minister says that he will take the report of the commission. Does he mean the comments or conclusions gathered by the commission, or the evidence itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My idea is this, that the information and reports of this commission will be departmental information, available for the government in considering tariff questions. Now that information, like all other information which is departmental, may be called for by this House, and may be laid on the table. I would be the last man to suggest that the House of Commons should be denied the information obtained by means of the expense which they have authorized. There is no intention of that kind in this Bill. My hon. friends have been simply raising spectres with regard to this Bill. The object of this Bill is to obtain information which could not be obtained in any other way. But because we propose to obtain information which hitherto has not been obtainable and cannot be obtainable otherwise, does not mean that the government seeks to be relieved from its constitutional responsibility for the tariff, and for tariff rates.

My hon.
friend, in his opening remarks, was kind enough to tell me that he would endeavour to meet my inquiry as to his idea of moderate protection.
I do not know that he has made the subject much clearer than it was. Perhaps it is clear to his mind. I wish I knew myself, but the difficulty is that nobody, whether in this country or any other country, has ever been able to draw the line between what is moderate protection and immoderate protection. I never knew a protectionist, not even the gentleman who stated in Toronto that he wanted the protective barrier against foreign goods to be as high as 'Hannanls gallows,' who ever pretended that he was anything but a moderate protectionist. The idea of the moderate
or immoderate protectionists with regard to protection is very much like the idea of the old squaw about whisky. Her idea was that a little too much was just enough. A little too much is just enough protection for the purpose of the manufacturer or of the man who is a moderate protectionist.
My hon. friend says that the object of this Bill is to have the facts. I agree with him that that ought to be the object of the Bill. It ought to be to get the. facts and nothing, else, and if I saw in this Bill evidence off an intention to have the facts and nothing but the facts, the truth and nothing but the truth, for my part, I would be satisfied with it. My hon. friend tells us that if we had had the facts there would have been no election on the 21st September, that we would not have been where we are now but where he is. Well, I must say, that looking at the long faces of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, there is a compensating feature to the fact that we were defeated on the 21st September. There is more joy on this side of the House than there is on the other side. I have noticed on several occasions during the present session that the faces of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have lengthened and lengthened until they were looking very much the picture of despair. Perhaps we may see the same thing again during the present session. I do not want my hon. friend to waste any pity on this side of the House; we are quite happy where we are and where hon. gentlemen will be some time or other.
My hon. friend tells us that if we had had the facts, as they had them in the United States, we would never have committed the imprudence that we did of making an arrangement with the United States. They have the facts in the United States, and we have not. But, if I am correctly informed, in the United States they collected the facts that they have without a Tariff Commission, and simply by a statistical bureau. I understand that they want a Tariff Commission in the United States just as my hon. friend wants to have a Tariff Commission here, but they were able to collect the facts with a simple statistical bureau such as they have now. I understand that in the United States, as ini this country, the dominant party is not satisfied with having a statistical bureau which will collect the facts and present them as they are, but that they rather desire to give a colour to them in favour of their own view, which is the view of the present administration. Of course, my hon. friend tells me that there is nothing of that kind in the Bill. Who expects to find anything of that kind in the Bill? There, is such a thing as an Act and an ulterior motive to that Act not to be found within the four

corners of the Act itself. My hon. friend did not put in his Bill that the object which he had in view was to have, not the broad facts as they exist, but simply a commission to prepare for him, and for the government of which he is a member, in favour of the view upon political economy which my hon. friend and his colleagues entertain. He did not tell us that, it is true, but we had an influential member on the other side of the House telling us that that was the intention of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

What is the meaning of these words spoken by the hon. member for Montreal St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) the other day? Speaking of the personnel of the commission he said, not that they must be high protectionists, but that they must be in sympathy with the well known sentiment of the present government. Well, if these are not partisans what are they? They may not be offensive partisans. It is difficult t-o lay down the line and say what is an offensive or an inoffensive partisan. Under the present administration we find that offensive partisanship is simply to ~be a partisan. These men who are to be apipointed commissioners under this Act, must be men who are in sympathy with the sentiments of my hon. friend. That is the qualification that was laid down by the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine. If I am told by my hon. friend (Mr. White) that the hon. member for Montreal is wrong, that he did not speak by authority, that he did not know what he was talking about, all I can tell my hon. friend is that until the words of the hon. member for St. Antoine have been disavowed by him, I will persist in believing that the members of the commission will be partisans and that they will be appointed with the object of supporting the views of my non. friend. My hon. friend tells us that we shall have the information. Certainly, we all agree to that, but he tells us also that we shall be the first to agree to this Bill which is to be put upon the statute-book, in order to get the information. He tells us that those who are against high duties ought to be in favour of this Bill. He tells us that there are men complaining to-day that the duties are too high, and that t-heir complaints should be investigated. Investigated by whom?

by men who are against high duties? No, by men who are in favour of high duties. That is the kind of justice that we are going to have. You are going to appoint a commission composed of men in sympathy with the present government. Men are men after all. We can all agree to this that we have our own passions, our own prejudices, and our own views. My hon. friend belongs to the legal profession, and he knows that in a court of law the Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
same fact may be presented by two men, who will give an entirely different colour to it, each of them honestly and acting in good faith. My hon. friend knows that men are unconsciously biased in favour of their own proclivities. Does he mean to tell me that when the facts are investigated by men who are of his own way of thinking, who are in favour of duties-call it moderate protection, if you like-you can expect from these men a report which will be in favmr of the converse view of no duty upon the articles under consideration? They would not be men, they would not be acting in accordance with the dictates of human nature, if it were to be supposed that under such circumstances they would give such a report. What alarms us in this matter, Sir, is that, as stated by my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), when speaking in answer to my hon. friend on the second reading of the Bill, you are taking this Yankee device, which has not yet become law in the United States, tout is intended to produce such an effect as to promote the view of the dominating party in the United States. The same thing must obtain here if you adopt the same methods.- That is the reason why I say that the Bill of my hon. friend is not intended, according to the statement of my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Antoine, to result in the preparation of an unbiased statement of the facts, but that it is intended to prepare a brief in every case for the administration in favour of the views which are held by my hon. friends opposite.
The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has stated to the House that if the purpose of the Bill were simply to provide information, he would be glad to support it.
Yes.
Would the right hon. gentleman suggest to the House what might be added to or substracted from the Bill that would make it such to his mind?
Simply to organize a statistical bureau such as they have in the United States and such as we have, to some extent, in this country.

The right hon. gentleman states that he would favour the Bill if it organized simply a statistical bureau such as exists in the United States. I have been at some pains to look into the legislation in the United States, to ascertain how the tariff board which exists at present, and which has existed for two years back is operated there, and I can see in it nothing more of the nature of a statistical bureau than that which is contemplated by the present Bill. The tariff board appointed by the President of the United States under the authority of the Customs

Act of 1901, is a tariff board designed for the purpose and with the powers of the Tariff Commission contemplated by this Bill, and has done work that is not of a statistical character at all, as well as work that is of a statistical character.
So that if the right hon. gentleman contemplated a board clothed with the power and having the objective of the tariff board of the United States, then he must be satisfied with this Bill as it stands, and I suggest to him that the Minister of Finance cannot devise an amendment either by addition or omission that will better provide for what the right hon. gentleman himself wants. Does the right hon. gentleman suggest that a definition of a moderate protectionist should be inserted in the Bill? The right hon. gentleman is greatly concerned this afternoon because he does not appear to know just what a moderate protectionist is. I suggest that he turn to the hon. gentleman behind him who has acknowledged to the House that he is a moderate protectionist and ask him what in the world he is. Then the hon. member for Richmond also made the same avowal to the House, and the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) refused to state that he would eliminate protection from our tariff, and I do not think he would say that if he is a protectionist. He is anything but a moderate protectionist.

I must protest against the hon. gentleman using a suggestion that was made in a previous debate to which it did not suit me at the moment to reply. But when the question comes up, if my hon. friend will bear with me, I will give him all the information.
I am at a loss to understand how the question can be up if it is not up now.
At all events I am not up at the moment, but I shall take care to be up and to enlighten my hon. friend.

He was up and very much up, and was enthroned in office for seven years, but then he was a protectionist just in the sense the late government was and that, I think, was moderate protection although in some cases it was immoderate, and in some cases not protection at all, just as political exigencies or necessity might dictate. The right hon. gentleman, surrounded as he is, and with the experience he has had, surely should be in a position if any man in the world is in a position, to define what moderate protection is.
The position as it appeals to me, is this. The tariff in this country must be framed on either one or another of two hypotheses. It must be framed to suit the fair exigencies of business and the people, or to suit the exigencies of politics. The
right hon. gentleman while he was leader of the government professed to adhere to to a policy of moderate protection, interweaving in some way with a tariff for revenue only, but he framed his policy, that is to say he drew the line where it would suit the exigencies of politics. I make that statement advisedly, and from having observed the policy of the right hon. gentleman, both as a' member of this House, and as a citizen of Canada. I do not think the right hon. gentleman will deny that that was the policy that guided him in the framing of his tariff. If I require further authority I read from an editorial in the Manitoba ' Free Press ', which is the organ of the right hon. gentleman in western Canada, and which strenuously conducted newspaper warmly supported him in the late contest.
My hon. friend honours me when he says that the ' Free Press ' is my organ.

I am always pleased to honour my right hon. friend when I can do so with truth. The editorial is headed ' A Permanent Tariff Board,' and contains the following sentence;
The late government was as protectionist as it thought it necessary to be to placate powerful interests and make them neutral or friendly.
Now that is the ta'lisman, according to the organ of the government itself, that regulated their protectionist policy. So that while the hon. gentleman who lately, represented western Canada, and whose views this doubtless interprets exactly, will, I hope, not disavow the authority of his organ in the west. If we are to follow that principle then the method adopted by the late government is beautifully suited to the case, authorizing a rambling band of politicians to pass over Canada and find out just what would be the political effect of a certain schedule here or there, and then fixing the schedule with a view to getting as large a percentage of votes as possible. That being the case, a tariff board certainly is an unnecessary luxury in Canada. But, if, on the contrary, we are to base our tariff on the business, commercial and industrial effects it will have, and so have the objective of the successful carrying on of Canadian industries and Canadian industrial 'life, we cannot have too much light, and no schedule in our tariff that cannot stand the light should stand without light, and on the other hand no schedule and no set of business people in Canada should be made to suffer the odium of ignorant suspicion in this country. That is the purpose of the tariff board. But hon. gentlemen want to know who the men on the board would be. There is not a responsible man on the opposite side who would

suggest that it was the duty of the government or of any one to assert now who the men would be. They say:	If we
do not know who they are, tell us their opinions. The hon. gentleman who sits behind the first minister has acknowledged that we know constitutionally no differences of party in this country and consequently it would be impossible, and not to be expected that the government would state from which party they were to come. The hon. gentleman is greatly' concerned about a statement of my hon. friend from St. Antoine division (Mr. Ames). No one in this House has more admiration for the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) than I have, and his conviction evidently is that most people in this country are, on tariff matters, in line with the government of the day. I think he has ample evidence to support his conviction because the great majority of the people in this country do believe in the policy of reasonable protection that is the policy ot this government.
The hon. member (Mr. Ames) made some remark from which the leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) draws the inference that he would debar a man if he had leanings towards free trade. For myself, if the appointee were qualified in every other way, if he came to the duties of his office with the qualifications which I think he should have, qualifications as a student and as a fearless investigator, qualified, in a word, as the minister has stated he should be qualified, then my opinion as a private member is that he should not be debarred from serving on the board. No minister has stated that any political opinion is to disqualify any man from serving on this board, if he is qualified fairly to investigate and to report, these are the qualifications insisted on by the government.
Now why should this Bill not pass?
Because the hon. member is keeping it back.
The hon. member says I am keeping it back. I feel quite confident that my hon. friend, when he comes to speak, will follow my illustrious example.

The Minister of Finance intimated that if there was more information the consumers of this county anight be more reconciled to the policy of reasonable protection. I think that is the key of the whole situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did I say that?

I regret very much if I have misinterpreted any statement of the hon. minister, but he said that what was needed was more information, and that if the consumers of Canada had more information perhaps they would be more reasonable in their attitude towards protection. That is

a paraphrase of what I understood the hon. Minister of Finance to say, that is the key of the situation. So far as one can gather from ministerial statements, this commission will be an institution for the purpose of gathering information of one kind With the object of inducing consumers to believe that they are wrong and that what is needed is more protection. It seems to me that that is a manifest deduction to be drawn from the speech of the Finance Minister. A year ago a commission was appointed for the purpose of getting information on the subject of technical education. That is a question in which different classes of the community are deeply interested. Had the leader of the late government proposed on that commission the representative of one particular class, such as the manufacturing interests, he would have been met by protests from all over the country.
When the Bill appointing that commission passed this House, were the names given of the men who were to be appointed?
They were not then, and I do not think anybody on this side has asked the present government to name the particular persons to be appointed.
Did anybody ask for a guarantee, when that commission wa= appointed, that the labour and other interests would be represented on it?

Whether that was asked or not is entirely beside the question. As a matter of fact all interests were represented on it. The manufacturers, the labouring men, the universities, were represented on that commission. Every interest likely to be affected by its proceedings and report was represented. Further than that I would remind my hon. friend that in the composition of that board, the Conservative party was not overlooked because in the appointment of Mr. Simipson >and Mr. Murray of Toronto, the late government named two men affiliated with the Conservative party.
I want to deny that. Mr. Simpson is an avowed Socialist.

From the experience I have in this House, I am quite prepared for interruptions from the hon. gentleman and do not take any account of them. But to come back to the question, what we desire is to have some guarantee from the Minister of Finance that the consumers of this country will be represented on this commission, and that it will not be an institution devised simply for the purpose of educating people into the belief that protection is the best policy for this country. If the sympathies of the men composing the commission should be entirely in favour of protection, we have reason to oelieve that they

[DOT] 2882
will be careful to summon before them only those who would be in sympathy with a higher tariff. As 1 pointed out the other evening, there is no provision in this Bill to enable a man to come forward voluntarily and give his evidence. It is provided that witnesses shall be summoned before this board to give evidence, but I submit that there should also be a provision enabling any man, no matter what may be his views on the tariff, to come forward and state them. The omission of such a provision justifies the conclusion that this institution is simply created to lead people into the belief that protection, and protection alone, is the proper policy for the country.
Does the hon. gentleman declare himself a free trader?

I do not know that whatever the hon. gentleman's views may be can have much significance, but, since he appears anxious to ascertain mine, I am in favour of such protection only as is necessary for the revenues of the country.

I must confess that I am much surprised at what I have heard from hon. gentlemen opposite. I thought that on the second reading of the Bill we had arrived at a conclusion as to what its real intention was, namely, to procure information for the government and the country in order that we might frame a. tariff measure suited to our needs. And let me say now that if there are hon. gentlemen more in need of information on that subject than any other they are to be found on that side. During the second reading of this Bill they exhibited the most extraordinary ignorance of the character of our tariff. I say that without any intention of being offensive, because they have been taught by their leader that the tariff in force is a low tariff, instead of which it is one of the highest taxation tariffs we have had during the last thirty or forty years. Go through it item after item of articles of every day consumption, and you will find the taxation on these increased enormously. Take the article of sugar, which is consumed by every family in the country, rich and poor. Now, if these hon. gentlemen, who plume themselves on being the low tariff party, were anxious to keep down taxation, why did they so enormously increase the duty on sugar? Raw sugar is the basis of the refined article, and the higher we increase the price of the raw the higher we raise the price of the refined. Hon. gentlemen opposite were not satisfied with the duty on raw sugar as they found it, but immediately on assuming office set to work to see how high they could make it. They told us that their tariff was for revenue only, and they were determined to get all
the revenue they could out of sugar. If we apply the tariff of the late government to the imports of sugar of the last year, we will find that they had increased the duty in 1911 on raw sugar alone by $344,000, which is a very considerable item for a low tariff government. It looks rather strange that they should be so extremely alarmed lest the Bill before the House should result in a higher tariff when they themselves have acted along that line by increasing duty after duty on articles of daily consumption.
Now, I say that there is no excuse for
that increased duty on sugar; and if as hon. gentlemen opposite say the Finance Minister is going to put somebody on this commission who will work along the line of increased duties, I think these hon. gentlemen should welcome it, because that has been their policy for many years. Without making special reference to what any hon. member said on the second reading of this Bill, I must say that I am amused at some of the statements made on the other side of the House on the subject of the tariff, for that subject came largely into the discussion. But let me point out a few concrete examples to show how far these hon. gentlemen are astray in their opinions of their own tariff. If these hon. gentlemen want a tariff in accordance with their ideals, and if they think that Tariff Commission will have the effect of raising the tariff, I think they should welcome this Bill instead of opposing it. But I do not think that is the intention of the Minister of Finance. He wants a commission sim*ply to give information. During the last fifteen years I have given great attention to the study of the tariff; in fact, I venture to say I have given as much attention to it as aiiy other hon. member of this House. I do not boast of it; it was my duty to do it. As a result of that study, I venture to say that, if any hon. member on that side thinks he has been supporting a lower tariff on many articles, he is sadly mistaken. And I believe that information to show how he is mistaken is what this \eommissitm will supply. I have given some instances of increased tariff in this House before, but let me call attention to a few of them now. Take the case of fire-arms. I was charged years ago with being a high protectionist by a gentleman who claims to be a free trader. But when I pointed out that his free trade principles carried him far above my idea of moderate protection in the rate of tariff duties, I think that hon. gentleman was quite surprised. When the late government came into power the duty on fire-arms was 20 per cent. Hon. gentlemen opposite immediately put it up to 30 per cent. That was not very like a free trade or lower tariff government..
Dangerous weapons.

Anyhow they thought they would put the tariff on a higher plane. Many people in this country wish to buy rifles and guns for hunting and that sort of thing, and they had to be taxed by this additional rate of duty. But the answer was that the British preference would regulate that. It would take one-third off the 30 per cent and bring it down to 20 percent, at which it had stood before. But they forgot we did not buy our firearms entirely from Great Britain, but largely from the United States. Firearms coming in from the United States or other countries pay 30 per cent duty, and only those coming from Great Britain enter at 20 per cent. I see, Mr. Chairman, you are looking at the clock, and I must be brief, otherwise six o'clock will arrive before we get through. But let us consider the clock for a minute. This is an instrument you will find in every household-abundance of them. Did the Liberal government, when it came in, leave the duty on clocks where it had been? No, they wanted ' tariff for revenue ' so they increased the duty on clocks. They said: Here is a thing that every man must have in his house, and here is a chance for us to get more money. And the same with watches. They knew that everybody in Canada desires to have a watch, so they said: We want revenue, so we will make them pay higher duty on their watches. I looked up the figures the other day to see what the increase was. The duty on watches under the much abused National Policy, had been 25 per cent. Hon. gentlemen opposite raised the duty to 30 per cent. But they said the British preference would regulate that, and bring the duty on watches a little below 20 per cent. But they forgot that Great Britain was not a watch making country. This is exactly one of the things in which our tariff commission could help. They would be able to tell us that Great Britain is not a watch making country, and thar consequently the hope of applying the British preference to the duty paid on watches will not be satisfactory. We get our watches chiefly from Switzerland, the United States and France. So, instead of paying 25 per cent on watches, as it was under the national policy, last year we paid over 28 per cent on watches from all countries, notwithstanding the British preference. Hon. gentlemen opposite have been supporting that tariff since 1897, and they are crying out to-day about the high tariff, when as a matter of fact this is the very tariff they made and supported. I might go on with item after item. Take linen goods. The duties were increased from 25 to 30 per cent. Of course, the British preference applied, but everything in this line that we Mr. HENDERSON.
get from countries outside of Great Britain came in at the higher rate of duty. Take even the grey cottons, which are made very largely in Canada. The duty was 22i per cent, but these hon. gentlemen, when in power, increased that duty to 25 per cent, of course, expecting the British preference to bring it down to 19 per cent. But the fact is that we do not get all our grey cottons from Great Britain. It is a fact known to every business man in Canada, that grey cottons made in Great Britain are not sold in Canada to any great extent. Why? because they are not so good. They are not of the same quality as the American and Canadian cottons, .and the people of this country will demand the American or Canadian goods in this line in preference to those made in Great Britain. They have to pay now 25 per cent instead of 22J per cent as it was before. But you may tell me that on the Canadian grey cottons of course there would be no increase, because they are made in Canada and do not pay duty.
Have we forgotten the theory of Sir Richard Cartwright and his friends, when they advocated so strongly, that if you place a tariff on an article of Canadian manufacture the price will just work up to the price of the imported article? That is the case, and there may be a great deal in it. Why, we are paying an increased duty price on al'l our Canadian made grey cottons. Take coloured cotton, 30 per cent under the o'ld government, raised to 35 per cent by the hon. gentlemen who are now crying high tariff, and who now dread a commission, a partisan commission that may be appointed that will increase the duty, .after having sat here ever since 1897 and supporting a high tariff. I am surprised that such is the case. But nevertheless, remembering what we heard during the second reading of the Bill, that seems to be the feeling of hon. gentlemen. After raising the duty on coloured cottons from 30 to 35 per cent, the government became alarmed, and reduced to 32i per cent, leaving it still 2i per cent higheT than under the National Policy. They thought that all our coloured cottons were coming from Great Britain, and were coming in under the reduced tariff. We do get a great many from Britain, but I tell you the best coloured cottons in every day wear by the women of this country are the coloured cottons made in Canada, no doubt about that. Take cotton prints for every day wear, the Canadian women want them and they will have them. They buy American prints, of course not high class prints, those they will buy from Britain, and the duty will be somewhat lower. That seems to me to be unfair. The preference is given to the woman who wants a high class article, but the woman who wants an article that will wear and wash, has to pay a higher

duty on it, practically. That applies to coloured cottons of every class. Take the men who wear ducks, denims and all these coarse goods that are used by the farmers, workingmen and the labourers for summer wear, they are all called upon to pay a higher duty by reason of this increase, because British goods of that class are not imported into Canada. You can go through the shops of Canada and you do not find ducks, denims, cotton tweeds and cotton-ades on their counters to -any extent, the people do not want them and consequently they are not to be found there. The result is that we have been paying during the last ten or fifteen years, duties on the articles that we do want, that the people want, a great deal higher than we did before. Why, then, all this alarm that the government is going to appoint a Tariff Commission that will be in favour of increasing the duties? Why, that is exactly along the line that hon. gentlemen have advocated and supported for the last ten or twelve years. I do not see why they should be alarmed about it. My hope is that the Tariff Commission that will be appointed will do away with a great many of these anomalies; it will have the effect of pointing out to the government the unfairness of a great many clauses in our present tariff along the line I have indicated. I am not finding fault. Hon gentlemen may say I am complaining about the British preference; nothing of the kind. But I say in many things it works against the interests of the people of this country, inasmuch as the duty on so many articles was abnormally increased before the British preference was made applicable to this country. It may be said that this whole discussion, perhaps, is a little aside of the Bill which is before us. But after hearing what hon. gentlemen opposite have said, who are so extremely alarmed that a high tariff is going to be the result of this commission, I thought that I could say something on the question. I am not alarmed that our tariff wall will be made higher; I am under the impression that the very effect of this commission will be to lower the tariff. We heard something this afternoon about some gentleman in Toronto having talked about a tariff as high as ' Haman's gallows,' and the insinuation was thrown out that that was the kind of tariff this commission was going to recommend. I hope the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition, and who made reference to that this afternoon, will not forget that the man who made that remark in Toronto was a Liberal friend of his own, not a Conservative.
No.

The Gurneys were , Liberals, there is no getting over that. It'
was Mr. Gurney who was the author of that statement, a friend of the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition.
Mr. Gurney was a Liberal, as the Minister of Finance is a Liberal.

Well, the Minister of Finance is a mighty good Liberal, I think; he is going to give hon. gentlemen more Liberal government than we have had for a great many years. But the late Minister of the Interior admits that Mr. Gurney was a Liberal when he made that statement.
No, no.

I remember well the criticisms about it and there is no getting over the fact that Mr. Gurney was a Liberal, and I am not aware that he ever changed his politics. I do not know how he voted, whether he voted for or against reciprocity, I never inquired into it. But on the question of the tariff, Mr. Gurney had been, a Liberal.
How long ago?
When he made this statement, and I am not aware that he changed his politics since.

The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) has stated that Mr. Gurney was a Liberal when he made that statement. Is it not correct that Mr. Gurney left the Liberal party in 1878 when the Conservative party introduced the policy of protection, and he has always been a Conservative from that time to the present?

I have lived near Toronto ever since 1878, and I never so understood it, and I believe the people of Toronto do not so understand it. I do not think Mr. Gurney is a Conservative today; if he is, I do not think his conversion has been thorough. Now strong objection was taken to something said I think, by the hon. member for St Antoine Montreal (Mr. Ames), and the inference was that he was recommending that partisans be appointed on this commission. Now what is a partisan?
Hear, hear; ask the Postmaster General.

Now I will ask the right hon. leader of the < ppos't ir fact I do not need to ask him, because I remember in this House when the right hon. gentleman, who was then leading the government, in discussing a question similar to this, said: Why, we are all partisans; he said that he himself was a partisan, and I do not think he has changed his mind. Has the right hon. gentleman forgotten that?
No.
He remembers that, he is a partisan, and we are all partisans. That does not apply only to the members of this House.
I am disqualified from sitting on this commission.
I think the hon. gentleman could hardly take that small exception. I understood the remarks of the right hon. gentleman at that time to apply to every man in the country. Who is the party man?
The Minister of Justice.

Yes, the Minister of Justice was, even judges on the bench, because it is very difficult to get rid of political feelings, but where are you going to find men to put on a commission of this kind if you do not take partisans?
They would be no use.

They would be no use because they would be men who had no opinions of their own. I do not wish to obtrude beyond the hour of six o'clock and I shall be very happy to give way to the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte).

I do not object to partisans being appointed to the commission, but I object to partisans from one party alone being selected.
