The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) has developed into the humoristic apologist for the low tariff ideas which prevail so markedly and so suddenly amongst those who sit on the government benches! In view of what the Minister of Finance has said with respect to the light that is to be thrown on the whole question of the tariff by this commission, and in view of the attitude taken by the hon. the member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) it is, I believe, an opportune moment to have light thrown on the course that is likely to be followed by the commissioners when appointed. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Ames) claimed that in view of the recognized policy of the present government, favouring a high protective tariff in Canada-
He did not say that.

Well, I do not wish to misquote what the hon. member (Mr. Mr. HENDERSON.
Ames) said, but I gathered from his remarks that there are three sqhools of economic thought in Canada, the free trade cult, the tariff-for-revenue cult, and those who advocate the protective theory, whether you call it high, low or moderate. The hon. member (Mr. Ames) took it for granted that in view of the attitude this government had taken for many years on their fiscal policy, the selection of members of the board would be from among those who favoured protection. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) was pleased to give utterance to some very witty remarks with respect to the attitude taken by members on this side, and these remarks read in contrast with some utterances of Sir Charles Tupper, leader of the opposition in 1896 and 1897, are undoubtedly humorous. When we recall the jeremiads and lamentations of Sir Charles Tupuer as respects the havoc that would be created in Canada by reason of the Fielding tariff in contrast with the prosperity of Canada under the so-called National Policy, the humour of the remarks of my hon friend will be quite apparent.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to say a word? He can recall, as I can, that the speech of Sir Charles Tupper to which he refers had reference to the first tariff brought down by Mr. Fielding ar.d not to the second tariff of the same year, which was a very different tariff.
Both tariffs were practically on the same lines, the difference being that the latter one provided for a greater reduction of duties.
Oh, no.

My hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), viewed the question from the exigencies of politics, but the exigencies of politics are one thing and the exigencies of the country are another. After all, it is not what tariffs have been in the past or what practice has been followed that we are interested in, so much as the course that is likely to be pursued under this new departure with respect to tariff creation. The Minister of Finance says that we on this side have created spectres and that we are fighting these spectres, but it seems to me that if spectres there be, they have been created by the utterances of the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), and of other supporters of the government. I asked a question of the Minister of Finance to-day about a rumour which was given wide currency in the eastern press which supports the government, and that rumour was to the effect that a member of this House, who represents a New Brunswick constituency, a lawyer by

profession-indeed I might name him, I refer to the hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket)-is to be appointed one of these commissioners. Now, when the resolution with reference to this Tariff Commission was first introduced by the Minister of Finance, he told us that he had in his mind ideals with respect to the experts-he used the word experts-who were to constitute this tariff board, and I gathered,from his remarks that we were to have an effort on the part of the government to create a scientific tariff board, and that qualified experts would be appointed with the view of recognizing all the interests of the country. I regret that the Minister of Finance failed to take the House into his confidence this afternoon, and to give his ideal as to the personnel of this board. The hon. gentleman has been charged with adopting a Yankee device in promoting this legislation, and it may be interesting to know what course has been adopted by the Congress of the United States, with re-stpeet to this same matter. In the very elaborate Payne-Aldrich Tariff Bill of 1909, there was nothing especially creating a Tariff Commission, but it had it it a very inrocent clause in these words:
To secure information to assist the president in the discharge of the duties imposed upon him by this section, (relating to the application of the maximum and minimum rates) and the officers of the government in the .application of the customs laws, the president is hereby authorized to employ such persons as may be required.
That clause in no sense created a Tariff Commission, but in pursuance of it appropriations were made to pay the salaries and expenses of the persons who might be appointed, and last autumn we are informed that these all told, amounted to over one hundred officials.
At first it was to be a body composed of three members. They had a staff of officials, experts and agents which Congress provided for them. It is interesting to know the character of the board constituted by President Taft, because he acted upon the authority of the Payne-Aldrich Bill. As chairman of the board he appointed Henry Crosby Emery, a Republican. He was formerly professor of economics at Yale University. He appointed as the second member of the board, James Burton Reynolds, who was a newspaper correspondent and editorial writer, a man in a quasi public position, .a strong Republican, connected with party management in one of the states. Then he appointed Mr. Alvin Howard Saunders, a prominent Republican in Illinois, owner and manager of the ' Breeders' Gazette,' a stock review in the central states, a man interested in stock raising. I may add that Mr. Reynolds was the assistant secretary of the treasury for four years in one of the Cabinets, where he had charge of customs affairs. He had also been chairman of the Parliamentary Reciprocity Tariff League. It was alleged that this was a partisan board, and it was the object of considerable criticism on that account. The President, in order to remove any ground for criticism, appointed two additional members to the board, because the Bill, under which he organized the board, did not fix any limitations as to the number. He appointed Mr. William M. Howard, a lawyer by profession, and a Democrat. He had, I think, held some public position which gave him particular knowledge with respect to tariff matters. The fifth member of the board was Thomas Walker Payne, a Democrat, a man of great ability and high standing, who had been formerly professor of economics at the University of California. Previous to that he was a teacher of economics in the University of Virginia, and at a later date, I think he was .connected with the University of Texas in a like capacity. There was a board consisting of three Republicans and two Democrats. Two of them were professors, one was a newspaperman, and two others were publicists, of whom one was a lawyer. Those gentlemen were ^supposed to be well qualified to aid as experts the government and President with respect to tariff matters. But this board did not even then come up to the ideal of those who had advocated the constitution of a nonpartisan board, and there has been a good deal of criticism of it, both on that ground and in respect to its power. Up to the present time it has aided the government by and through its staff in gaining information. It is true that in procuring this information they relied more upon their experts tind officials, and practically it would be on the same footing as if the department of my hon. friend were to create a staff of experts to procure for him the information which this board procured for the President of the United States through their experts and agents. Since then, Congress has made two efforts to create a Tariff Commission apart from this Tariff Board. One Bill was introduced by the Republicans, .and another by Democrats, but neither Bill has made much progress up to this time. Now it will be admitted that the people of the United States were seeking some such body as I have described. The object of the board was undoubtedly to 'eliminate special privileges which were supposed to be favoured by the tariff. The object in view, as stated by the President and understood by the people, was to secure information which would justify the elimination from the tariff of all special privileges. Now, they have not yet accomplished that object.

There is a suspicion that the object of a Tariff Board such as is eonstitued by this Act is not to eliminate any special privileges, but to create special privileges iu favour of this or that particular class. In view of this suspicion, whether it is well-founded or not, we should have information from the minister if not with respect to the actual personnel of the commission, at least as to the class of men who are to be appointed. If the appointees are to be politicians, men who have been closely identified with the tariff policy of the party now dominant in this country, then this Bill merits very severe criticism at the hands of the members of this House and I am sure it will be severely criticised if not condemned by the people of Canada. A witty writer in speaking of the Tariff Board of the United States compared them to setting hens, and asked: What will the Tariff Board hatch? The minister, in saying that we have no right to ask at this stage for the information for which we have asked should bear in mini that what will be hatched will depend very materially on the character of the eggs which are to be placed under this board. If they be high tariff eggs, and if the commission is appointed to seek out devices whereby due privileges can be given to special classes, the proposal would be strongly condemned by the people of Canada. If a man is particularly interested in one class of industry he is likely to favour that class as a member of the board. I hold that the manufacturing interests are not alone interested in the tariff, that the great consuming body in Canada are entitled to have representation on that board and I think the minister would be doing himself great justice if he would candidly say to the consuming classes of Canada that it is his purpose to see that their interests shall be represented - on this Tariff Commission when he makes a selection of the members of that board.
Would the bon. gentleman then support the measure?

My hon. friend cannot answer my question by asking another one. The responsibility with respect to this Bill does not rest on me. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has placed upon himself the responsibility of creating the board in the interests of the whole of Canada. If a board should be created representing all interests in Canada then the fears and alarm felt by the consuming class throughout Canada

Mr. CURRIE Would the hon. gentleman tell us who are the consuming classes apart from the producers in this country?
Is the hon. gentleman in favour of some tribunal investigating these conditions?

I am not framing a Bill, I am not inviting my hon. friend to consider any Bill that I am proposing, I am discussing this Bill and I say it does not go far enough. If the hon. gentleman wants to know my views on economics, I may tell him that I am a free trader in every sense of the word.
Since when?
I have been a free trader for a long time, but I recognize that it was impossible to make a sudden change to free trade. The day will come, however, when that policy will prevail in Canada.
Never.

The silent member has spoken. We are tola by that silent modest retiring gentleman, the member from Simcoe, that we are never to have anything nearly approaching free trade. I suppose that settles the question. But after all we are dealing with this Bill as to its possibilities and the fruits it may bear in the future, it is not a matter of material moment whether this one or the other favours free trade or a tariff for revenue only or protection pure and simple. But it is a matter of supreme importance to the people whether, in constituting this commission, we are creating an agency that will act in the interests of the manufacturers, and erect greater barriers in favour of the privileged classes against the welfare of the people. If there is anything in this Bill tending in that direction, it should be eliminated.
There should be every opportunity given to discuss this Bill clause by clause, minutely, and, if possible, to remedy it. I assume that it makes no difference what my opinion in respect to the Bill is.
Hear, hear.

I say ' hear, hear ' to that, because I know that my hon. friend proposes to put it through and he has a ready and willing sutpporter in the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) and other members who are quite willing to nod just as he beckons. I take it for granted that this Bill is going through whether we are in favour of it or not. But it is of great importance as to whether the people of this country will favour a measure of this kind which will have, even if not intended, the result of affecting the interests of the consumer. The farming and consuming classes , are compelled to buy in the dearest mar-

ket, and in whose interest? In the interest of the manufacturer and only recently, on the 21st September, we denied to the producers the privilege of selling in the best and the widest market. So, they are clipped at both ends. We have given them a hobble skirt. We have hobbled them on all sides and now all through the country they are hobbling along by reason of the attitude of this government and the party which supports it. If this measure is to go through, I want this hobbling removed and as hobble skirts are not in favour in the fashionable world
Hear, hear.

Yes, and as they are not in favour in the fashionable world, so is our hobble skirted policy with respect to the tariff not in favour among the consuming classes of Canada and the sooner the government realize that, it will be very much better for them and, regardless of the benefits which might accrue to them, it will be very much better indeed for the .people of Canada.
That is right.
My hon. friend agrees with that old policy? [DOT]
Yes.
I am sure that a very large majority of the people of Canada differ from my hon. friend on that point.
It is not a large one.

And I would say to my hon. friend and the Liberal opposition, that whatever impression they were able to make on the fanners of Canada in the years gone by, they. will not be able to make any now. The farmers have reuliz-Mr. EMMERSON.
ed that there is no class of people in Canada who have benefited to a greater extent by the National Policy, if you might call it that, than the farmers themselves. They have built up in Canada, under the sc-called National Policy, put upon the statute-books by the Liberal-Conservative party and continued in the main by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in office-a splendid home market.
It must have been very sick for about eighteen years.

My hon. friend has argued it from that standpoint, but I am arguing it now from the standpoint of the Bill before the House. The farmers pronounced on the 21st September upon that question. The policy of the late government, when introduced, was a bid for the farmers' vote. They threw out the policy of partial reciprocity between Canada and the United States and it made a distinct issue in the last election that ended on the 21st September, with what result? With the result that the farmers all over Canada, almost in every part, turned to the Liberal-Conservative party >and said: We will give you our support, and they did it on the 21st September last.
They are sorry for it now.

I may say to my right hon. friend (.Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that his Minister of Militia came up from the battle on the 21st September and, when interviewed in the city of Montreal and asked the question : How do you account for the defeat, said:	In my county the farmers went
against me.
They are sorry for it now.	.
The only sorrow I see in Canada anywhere is on the other side of the House.
No, no.

My hon. friends have not and cannot discuss any question since this House assembled ,a few months ago without introducing the reciprocity proposition in some part of the debate, showing that whatever else may have been on their minds there is this important question upon their minds which was settled on the 21st September.
You would like to have it forgotten.
I am a frank protectionist. I am not ashamed of that position, and the farmers who sent me here are protectionists too.
Moderate or immoderate?

I am for moderate protection, of course. We have never had a man in this House who was a protectionist to say that lie was anything else than a moderate protectionist. I was looking over the tariff the other day that was in force when the Liberal-Conservative party were in office before, and I made some comparisons between that old tariff and the boasted Fielding tariff of 1907. Go over item after item and you will find that in many cases items that lion, gentlemen condemned for so many years while they were in opposition and condemn now are exactly the same as in the Fielding tariff that they boasted so much of. Take, for instance, the article of apples; 40 cents a barrel was the duty put on long years ago. That was condemned by hon. gentlemen opposite. They said: Of course, protection cannot protect the farmer; but when they came into office and brought down the boasted Fielding tariff the same old duty of 40 cents a barrel was placed on apples. They condemned it when they found it had been placed upon the statute-book by the Liberal-Conservative party and applauded it when they left it as it was in the measure of the Liberal government. This question of establishing a Tariff Commission was introduced into Canada only a few months ago, but in reality it had been referred to in this country and in the House for many years.
When it was mentioned, some months ago, before the House assembled the newspapers took it up. The newspapers on either side of politics understood what was meant, and nowhere did they take from it what hon members on the other side take from it, that it is a Bill designed to take away legislative powers from the government of the day. In proof of this, let me cite an editorial from the Toronto ' Globe ', a newspaper that would not be too friendly to this government. On January 6 last, the Toronto ' Globe ' said, referring to the Tariff Bill:
The Canadian Commission will have no executive functions, and will in no way usurp the right of parliament to regulate 'imposed duties. It will report to the government findings of fact and evidence upon which the same are predicated, and these will .be laid before parliament in justification of such fiscal changes as may from time to time be proposed by the government.
So the ' Globe * understood it very well, for it points out the very substance of the Bill the Finance Minister has introduced. It does not for a moment suggest that this Bill will take away any functions of the government or of this parliament. It is understood that the functions of the Tariff Commission will be to lay before parliament for the use of every member, and I suppose particularly for the use of the 92
Cabinet ministers now in office, such important facts as are necessary for an understanding of any proposals to alter the tariff. Surely, that is something that commends itself to every man. Surely it will commend itself to that class of people who suggest that the manufacturers of this country are too highly protected. To hear hon. gentlemen opposite when mention is made of manufacturers, one would think that the manufacturers were the enemies of this country instead of its friends. I do_ not think it becomes any member of this House to cast reflections on the manufacturing class whose members are to be found in both parties and who paid last year no less than $250,000,000 in gold in wages to the people of Canada. They do not require any defence on my part; they are well able to take care of themselves. Imagine the manufacturers of Canada, who have their money invested, who watch their business closely, and enterprisingly seek a market for their products, coming to the Finance Minister and suggesting to him to put on the statute-book a protective policy, as hon. members opposite would _ call it, diametrically opposed to every interest of the farming class in Canada. The farmers are the main customers of the manufacturers.
Without the home market afforded by the farmers, the manufacturers of Canada could not succeed. I cannot see how any man on either side can suggest-I doubt that any man really would suggest-that the manufacturers would come to the doors of parliament demanding such increases of duties as hon. members on the other side speak of to kill off the farming industry of this country. I believe that the farmers are interested in the tariff and that the manufacturers are equally interested. I believe that hon.. members on the other side are in favour of tariffs-they proved themselves so by keeping the National Policy on the statute-book. It was a debatable question in this House what changes they would make on coming into power in order to keep the pledges that they had given to the people years before. They failed to keep those pledges. And I do not think the people of this country will take them at their word any more. For my part, I am thinking the Bill should commend itself to this House, and I am sure it will commend itself to the people. If there is a manufacturing establishment now that has the benefit of protection higher. than it should have, the duty of the Tariff Commission will be to gather such information in respect of that establishment and manufacture, and lay it before parliament and the people so that the case may be understood. That is all my hon friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White, Leeds) is asking. And I think



it will be time enough for hon. members on the other side to condemn the Tariff Board when it has been in operation and has made some mistake. It is all very well for hon. members opposite to declare that they are seeking information. The leader of the opposition declared in this discussion that he was anxious for facts. He was crying for information because my right hon. friend said that when we were discussing the (reciprocity proposition ta few months ago there was seme suggestion that we of this country did not have sufficient information, that we suffered in that respect in comparison with the legislature on the other iside of the line which had complete information. I think my hon. friend is correct in that we did complain of lack of information. Some hon. members suggest now that they want information, but that information could be had in some other way. In what other way? By adding to the staff of the Finance Department. Would not that cost money? The only difference is as to whether these new officers should be called a Tariff Commission or whether they should be called officers of the Finance Department to gather these statistics and lay them all on the table. That is a small matter, so small that I do not think the hon. members opposite will interest the people of Canada in their criticisms. Looking over the Bill, its simplicity appeals to me. This commission is to investigate
(a)	The price and cost of raw materials in Canada and elsewhere, and the cost of transportation thereof from the place of production to the place of use or consumption.
That has always been a subject of discussion when tariffs are before the House:
(b)	The cost of production in Canada and elsewhere ;
(c)	the cost of transportation from the place of production to the place of use or consumption, whether in Canada or elsewhere;
(d)	the cost, efficiency and conditions of labour in Canada and elsewhere;
(e)	the prices -received by producers, manufacturers, wholesale dealers, retailers and other distributors in Canada and elsewhere;
(f)	all conditions and factors which affect or enter into the cost of production and the price to the consumers in Canada.
Hon. gentlemen opposite say there is nothing in the Bill relating to consumers. Surely this is a reference direct enough. And why should not the Finance Minister be as much interested in the consumer as hon. gentlemen on the other side? The Minister of Finance and his colleagues will -have to report in a few years to the people of Canada. I should think that the Minister of Finance would be as much interested in the consumer as any hon. gentleman on the other side who has no Mr. BLAIN

I do not know any civilized nation that has	ever taken	that position,
t(hat has ever adopted absolute free trade, trade unrestricted in any respect whatever. It is not pretended that free

England collects a large revenue.
Does England collect any revenue on material produced in England?

I was just coming to that. The point I was trying to make is that you may have a tariff for revenue and have eliminated from that tariff all principle of protection. That is the sort of revenue tariff, as I understand it, that is practised in England. England collects a large revenue from imports into England consisting of things that are not produced in England. England is consistent as a revenue tariff country and from that tariff is eliminated all principle of protection. As my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) knows very well, that is the principle of free traders. They take the ground that if they are to raise a revenue at all they are to collect that revenue upon imports of articles that are not produced in the country. As an illustration of that you have in England a tax of 10 cents a pound on tea. Is there an hon. gentleman in this House who will say that he is in favour of a tariff of that kind from which the principle of protection is entirely eliminated? Not by any means. Hon. gentlemen opposite never attempted to introduce a tariff of that kind. They went up and down this country from the time that Sir John Macdonald introduced the National Policy resolutions in this House in 1876, until 1896- twenty years- leading the people to believe that if they were successful at the polls they would introduce the principle of free trade. But, when they came into power they proceeded to practise protection, they have practised it ever since and they are in favour of it to-day; that is in the sense that they are not in favour of eliminating from our tariff the principle of protection.
