I suppose they were all partisans. They went about the country, and manufacturers and others appeared before them, each man who appeared before them presenting his particular view of the

matter. Then, we had a revision of the tariff in 1897, and we had three members of the right hon. gentleman's cabinet going about the country, and I suppose they were partisans just as the committee of the Conservative Cabinet in 1893, went about the country, partisans, gathering up evidence. Again, in 1907, the Liberal government sent three members of the Cabinet, three partisans, through the country to procure information with regard to the revision of the tariff. So it is admitted by all that it is essential, before dealing with the tariff, to secure special information with regard to it. The methods that we have heretofore adopted have been to send out three or four partisans to get that information, and yet the right hon. gentleman objects to this board, because, he says-, it will be composed of partisans. We have nothing but partisans heretofore going "about looking for such information. This board will not only get facts, but they will investigate, they will inquire, they will not accept the statements of gentlemen, perhaps manufacturers or others, who desire a particular duty placed upon a particular article. They will investigate and inquire into all the facts, they will find out what the article costs, what proportion of the cost of production is and should be assigned to wages. I am specially interested in that. I would like to know what proportion of the cost of any article should be assigned to wages. So, we must boil it all down to this question, whether we are to have an independent board who will inquire and investigate and get at the bottom of things, or whether we shall endeavour to get at the information as we have done heretofore by three or four members of the government going about the country, and in a desultory manner getting such facts and views as they could from different parties interested in regard to the tariff. There seems to be no ground whatever, for objection to this Bill, and I think it should be accepted at once.

Mr. Chairman, my fear is the very opposite of the hope which has been expressed by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers).
He expresses the hope that the Tariff Commission would get down to the bottom of things; my fear is that it will get the tariff up to the top of things. My hon. friend threw out a very curious challenge when he knew that my humble personality was on this side of the House- I rather think he withdrew that challenge afterwards in my own particular case, but for fear it might be still standing I accept it with cheerfulness and I hope with courage and with the ability to give a good reason for 'accepting it. The hon. gentleman said: was there any hon. gentleman Mr.'CROTHERS.
on this side of the House who could go in for what he vex'y correctly described as a tariff for revenue only. Well, I would and for this most obvious reason; that the tariff is a system of taxation, and we are all seeking science in a system of taxation. Now, when you collect on things that are only made outside of Canada, everything you take except the expenses of collection goes to the revenues of the country and, therefore, that is an approach at any rate, to a scientific system of taxation. When you put a tariff upon an article produced in the country, you collect duties for the country, and so far so good; but you collect two revenues, you collect another revenue for the interested minority inside the country. It is to the second revenue I object as toeing the most unscientific thing in taxation that one can conceive. I would like to say a word or iwo about the very interesting remarks made by my hon. friend, from Peel (Mr. Blain). I always like to hear my hon. friend, and sometimes he has followed me in debate and I was mt even then very much put out by him, but the boot is on the other foot to-night, and I certainly will not try to put him out by anything but fair argument. I was very much struck with what seemed to have occurred to him, namely, that the tariff is still and constantly with us. I think that is a most peculiar circumstance; it is a curious thing that the tariff is everywhere. I read a paragraph in a leading paper in the United States the other day, which said:	Congress will have most of its time this year taken up with the tariff; Congress has had most of its time taken up by the tariff for the last throe .yelars. Heirs, we in Canada have talked tariff fior twelve months, fought the hardest and best-nat-ured battle we could on tariff, and we come back to parliament and we meet tariff again. It is peculiar; I agree with my hon. friend. He says the tariff will be with us for many years, and I say it will be with us until it is treated in the only way it is proper to treat it, and that is with a bludgeon. The only thing to iiand out to the tariff is a club, and when it is treated in that wav, you will gc-t rid of it, at any rate for a long time. It is perfectly true, that in the fifty years during which Britain was so busy building up i world trade which will baffle all readers of all future times, she could not attend to tariff matters at all; it is perfectly true that after fifty years a very great statesman was able to get some thought concentrated upon it, but- I think the people are over-hopeful who at the present moment are looking for a return to protective principles in Britain.
It is a very unwise thing to prophecy, but I will prophecy that Germany will be

a free trade country before Britain returns to protection, and I make that prophecy with, I think, some kind of authority, based on the marvellous results of the recent elections in Germany. As I have said, it strikes me as being most peculiar that this government, of all others, should be dealing with tariff questions at this moment, because we have just fought an election, and we fought it on a specific principle on the ipart of hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the House, laid down by the leader of their party who is now Prime Minister of the Government. One of the strongest points in the right hon. gentleman's speech in this House was: Let well enough alone. Well, why is not the government doing it; are things not well enough? The position of the government is the most vastly illogical I can conceive. They have won the election and they all proclaim (that rproteiction won it; then why have they not the courage of their convictions to put the tariff up? What are they frightened about? However, that is anticipating what I am going to say. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) also made a very impassioned defence of the manufacturers of the country. I cannot understand his point of view; of course, I suppose he cannot understand mine. He said: these gentlemen have put their capital into their business. Where did they get the capital? Well, just ias the consumers have got a very much smaller amount, by making it for themselves, the only way a self-respecting man wants to get capital. I tried to teach in a little debate the other day, in which I am afraid I was misunderstood by some of the workingmen of the country, the idea that you will only have good workingmen when you teach them to be self-supporting, but I have more sympathy with the workingman than with the manufacturer, who wants to lean upon the shoulders of a bolstering and supporting government. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain), occupies a little more detached position than some of his colleagues, he does not have that seat in the Cabinet which many of us w'ould have liked to have seen him have, and I do not for one moment, say that as a taunt. But, the hon. gentleman (Air. Blain) used to be a very active member of the Opposition side of the House, and I want to argue with him on this question and to try to make my position clear to him. He looks at the interests of the manufacturers; while I look upon the interests of the consumer, entirely so, and I do it on a very simple principle, I can find it in Adam Smith, and I can find it in almost the same words in Bastiat. They both lay down the principle, the end of all production is consumption. I do not think there is a man or boy in Canada to-night who does not believe that this is obviously true. If the
end of all production is consumption, and if you look after the consumers, you are looking after everybody. That is the difference between my point of view and the point of view of my hon. friend from Peel. Is it not as clear as a sunbeam at mid-day that if you see that you have plenty ot consumers in your country, and plenty of things that they consume, there will be nothing wrong with the producers? If you have consumers in great numbers there will always be plenty of consumption and the producers are the natural consequence. I do not feel that I need, in this informal discussion, go further into the subject of the general position of free trade versus protection. I am sorry that my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) is not in the chamber, but I know he will do me the honour to read what I say about him in ' Hansard.' I always like to see him rise in the House; I like the lineaments, of his face, and I like him -when he goes on to show up what I must confess are the variegated views of the (party, even on this side of the House. But I wanted to tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) that I am not at all sure that he is not the real Diabolus in this play. We all remember that when he was once asked in this House, he was then sitting in Opposition, what he would do about the British preference, he made no bones about the kind of protection he believed in; there was no sentiment about him. He replied: you give me fifty of a majority on the government benches, and I will soon let you see what I will do with the British preference.
May I again appeal to the courage of my hon. friends opposite. If those are their opinions, why do they not carry them out? If they are not their opinions, why do they seek to put the subject on one side by. referring it to a Tariff Commission? We have heard a good deal of the need of information. Well, we cannot have too much information; I concede that point very readily. We have, however, some information on tariffs, and on tariff commissions already. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance interests me. I have heard the hon. member described as a moderate protectionist. Well, Sir, they all begin that way; the becoming of a full-blown protectionist is a rake's progress, they all begin in that fashion. I remember very well Mr. Alorley pointing out, when Mr. Chamberlain first began his propagandism in England, that in France they put the molest little duty of 1 shilling and 10 pence on flour, and said there would never be any reason to raise it. There was soon a duty of 12 shillings, an increase of 500 per cent. All protectionists begin as moderate protectionists. I am afraid I would have to describe myself as an immoderate antiprotectionist, because I reaffirm my strong belief in the club as the proper way to deal

with all tariffs. We have some facts about the tendency of tariffs, and we have these facts as to the tendencies of tariffs under commissions. I have given a fact as I could give many others, as to the tendency of tariffs, which is nearly always to rise. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) has tried to prove that that happened under the government of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), and with men struggling in the strength of their low tariff ardour to ho'ld the tariff down, if the rates rose under such aegis and protection, what route would they naturally take when they have their friends behind them? How can they do anything but rise? I should be very much mistaken if I should be successfully contradicted when I say that the tendency of tariffs is to rise under commissions, and that that was proved to the hilt in the countries of Germany and the United States, which have always been the countries from which supporters of protection have derived their main argument. You appoint your commission, up goes the tariff.
Does the hon. gentleman say that applies to the United States?
As far as my information goes.
It must go a very short distance.

I would like to have successful contradiction. I said the kind I wanted was successful; I did not know that there had been any reduction in the United States since the time a tariff was first made. When were the reductions made?

The hon. gentleman stated that wherever a commission was appointed, the tariff went up and that that applied to the United States. I contradicted that. I wish plainly to state -that I am right and my hon. friend is wrong, that the tariff has not gone up in the United States since the commission was appointed, and furthermore, every recommendation based on the commission's report has been for a revision downwards.
Will my hon. friend be good enough to specify some of the articles which have been reduced by the action of the commission, and will he state in addition that there has been no rise in the tariffs?

I shall state positively that there has been no rise. The Payne-Ald-rich tariff went into effect in 1909, and under the same Act that put that tariff into effect the Tariff Board was appointed. Since that tariff went into effect there has been no rise. The hon. gentleman for Red Deer stated the contrary. On the facts adduced Mr. CLARK (Red Deer).
by the Tariff Commission, and I refer specifically to wool, known as schedule 'K' in the Customs Act, the President of the United States has made strong recommendations to Congress for the reduction of the wool schedule.
It has not been done.
It haj not been done, but the commission in so far as it has interfered has endeavoured to have it brought down and it is only a matter of time.

I am very glad that my hon. friend has been able to prove that in the United States a Tariff Commission has actually produced a recommendation for a reduction, I am glad to have my information on the tariff increased.
May I refer to the pulp and paper schedules in which a reduction has actually taken place?
That had nothing to do with the recommendation of the board.
The board reported on the schedule.
That happened as part of an arrangement of which my hon. friend was one of the most bitter opponents.
What difference does that make?
Are you prepared to retract what you said to the effect that wherever there was a Tariff Commission appointed the duties had gone up, and your reference to the United States?
If my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie says he has handed his honour and his ability to conduct a debate over to the Minister of Labour, I will do anything that he says.
That js not answering the question.

I would remind my hon. friend that this is the second time he has had to be reminded of that kind of thing, because the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk) told him emphatically one evening that he felt quite equal to looking after himself.
I ask you whether you would retract the statement I have quoted?

If everybody on that side of the House including the Minister of Labour was as anxious to learn the true facts on the tariff question, three-fourths of the people of Canada would be free traders at the next election.
That is no answer.

It is a genera! statement which conveys an answer, it tells

my hon. friend of an honest and bpen mind. Does 'he think I wiant to gain a single point in debate or in my position on the tariff question by making a statement which I know to .be false? If I think it is right, why what can I do to retract it, but I am going to reiterate the statement and I am going to say that the evidence drawn from the United States is an extremely slight one, as to the tendency of tariffs under commissions. It is a certainty they went up permanently in Germany. They could not go up much higher in either Germany or .the United States. With two-thirds of the people in Germany becoming Socialists and two-fifths of those in the United States (becoming paupers, it is .extremely difficult to say" what the course of the tariff will .be in the future.
The Minister of Finance referred to this S3 a pillow fight. After he has had a little more experience of tariff debates in this House and is a little more able to take care of himself, than he can possibly be now although his abilities are very great, we will give him as much as he likes but he need not be afraid of suffering from too much pillow fighting on this question. He spoke of it being a bogey. It is a bogey if a bogey is a thing that frightens. YTou* talk about new facts. We have too many facts. He proclaimed his belief in the new facts and followed that by a reference to the election of September 21st.
He said that if we had known more facts then we would not perhaps have had that election. Well, I can only inform him and the government that we know more facts in the west now. I received a letter this morning from a friend of mine, an intelligent farmer in my own constituency. It comes from a part of the ^country where is to be found the finest land in Alberta. It was written by a sturdy, strongdieaded Scotsman originally, who was for many years in the United States .and came to western Canada, when so many other men in the United States, came over. He tells me that ninety per cent of the inhabitants there would be anxious to-day to sell their holdings at $10 an acre less than they would have been induced to take for their land by any means before the 21st of September last. My hon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) smiles incredulously, but of course he has, no regard for the farmers on the prairie. His regard is limited to the lumber combine of British Columbia. My hon, friend from Peel (Mr. Blain.) said that reciprocity Jay heavily on our minds, and this intelligent farmer in my constituency tells me in his letter that the wheat is lying heavy on the prairie. How can you expect to make Canada a great and successful country by means of a ridiculous economical fiscal policy of that kind? Can you not see that
we are more likely to make Canada the prosperous country she ought to be by filling the stomachs of hundreds of poor families in the slums than by building up multi-millionaires in the palaces of" our cities. I see that I am exciting some interest among hon. gentlemen opposite, and I have no doubt that in a little time we may succeed in getting some sound ideas accepted by hon. gentlemen opposite, because they are not had-hearted men, but just a little wrong-headed on this question.
Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to read that letter?

My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition has it. I do not expect credence from imy hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples), but if he wants to challenge imy .statement I am quite willing to accept his challenge and let the House judge between us.
I only wish to point out that when .an hon. gentleman refers to a letter or any other document, he may be called on to quote it and put it on record in 'Hansard.'

For my hon. friend's information and that of the House, I would point out that a few days, or it might have been a few weeks-and a few weeks are only .a few days in the history of a country-before September 21 there were 600 inquiries sent to a real estate office as to the value of lands and the opportunities for investment and immigrat'on to that part of the country, but since the election those inquiries have dwindled down -all told to 24. I need hardly point out to hon. members of this House, whose fathers were pioneers in this country, trying to make an honest living out of it, that it is all very well to 'build up millionaires, but you will never build up a strong, prosperous country unless you have strong yeomen on your farms, and you cannot have these unless you give them a square and fair deal in this matter. Facts are" what we want, and I have given a few.
I now come to close quarters with this proposition for the establishment of a tariff commission. It is the business of government and parliament to get the facts for themselves. Imagine Mr. Gladstone or Mr. Goschen, or Lord Randolph Churchill, or Mr. Low, or Sir Robert. Peel, or Mr. Lloyd George, or Mr. Asquith, all Chancellors of the Exchequer within the last two generations-imagine their being told, that they should appoint a commission to do those things which it is essentially the function of parliament and governments to do. When I came to this country Mr. Fielding with other members of the government, of which he was a distinguished member, were members of a temporary

commission-very different from that which we are appointing under this Bill, which is to be a permanent one. Mr. Fielding has gone from this House now and has left behind him no personal enmity but many strong admirers. When Mr. Fielding went about the country on that temporary commission he showed on many occasions that he knew more about the business of the men who appeared before him than they even knew themselves. In that respect he was superior to other members of the board which is a criticism that I know will commend itself to hon. gentlemen opposite. One gentleman who appeared before that commission in connection with the tariff on dried apples, said he was as quick as a needle and knew everything about that subject. It was his duty to know it for the information of his own department.
Dried apples?

There are some interruptions, Mr. Speaker, which I must pass over in silence. We had in Mr. Fielding an example of greater industry than we have had in parliament this long while. My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) introduced into this House a resolution in favour of free agricultural implements. If imy memory serves me rightly my h'on. friend corrected me brfore, and he now has an opportunity to set me right if I have not accurately stated his resolution.
I am sorry that I shall again have to correct my hon. friend.
What then did my hon. friend do? I guarantee it is not what he is going to do now.

I would have thought that the hon. member for Red Deer, before discussing what I did would have tried to know what really was the resolution I did move on that occasion to which he refers. That resolution was to the effect that in my judgment the time had come when the agriculturists of Canada were entitled to substantial reduction on farm implements, such as would not, under the circumstances, be inconsistent with a protective tariff.

I stand corrected with all the grace possible, but let me tell my hon. friend that in every western constituency, where I took any part in the last election, certainly in my own, every three cent advocate-and I am not using that expression in a professional sense-of anti-reciprocity said that Mr. Borden, if elected to power, would give this immense boon of free agricultural implements.
I should not be surprised if there were three-cent advocates-again not in a professional sense-in the constituency of Mr. CLARK (Red Deer)
Portage la Prairie to promise some things of that kind on behalf of my hon. friend. However, the question about the terms of the resolution is a small one. My point is that he made a speech in support of that resolution, a speech which I oo not know7 I have any great reason to admire. For he was not very kind to me at the beginning. He referred to me in a way that hurt me, andi I have always regarded with favour a dictum of Cardinal Newman that a gentleman, even if he have not the term ' hon.' b.efore his name, wall not willingly wound any man. The hon. gentleman called ane an ' exotic.' Mr. Chairman, I have observed that if ever I want a slur upon the person of the Englishman or the policy of England, I must always go to the English party in this country for it; I have not got it on the other side. However, I was not very much put out, I would like to tell my hon. friend. But I was a good deal more put out than I would have been if he had brought his resolution on at a time when w7e could all have debated it, for if I had had a chance to reply to him, I should not have been put out-at least, I would have tried to do as much putting out as was done to me. After all, the term was not a very worthy one. The question of a man's views on protection and free trade is not a question of whether those' views do or do not come from England. If they do come from England, are they any worse for that in the eyes of hon. gentlemen who, forsooth, have just refused to have truck or trade with the Yankee, because they are such Englishmen? Why, then, should a man or opinion be called ' exotic,' because he or it comes from England? The question is, does the man stand lor freedom, does he stand for truth, does he stand for justice? If he and his views stand for freedom, truth and justice, I want to tell my hon. friend that the more ' exotics ' of that kind you get into Canada the better. But I want to tell him also that truth and justice and freedom are not exotics^ in Canada, though we could do with a little more freedom-a great deal more freedom -on the trade question.
We have a speech made by the hon. member, I listened to that speech, and it seemed to me very admirable and very convincing; that was not very difficult for he had a favourable audience when talking of reduction of tariffs. But he was kind to the House. He told us the mechanism of the speech, the process of its manufacture. He said: I collected these statements tnyself. So, we knew how he went about it. I am not criticising my hon. friend; he must not be uneasy, I am commending him. He did these things himself, he told us, and he produced an admirable and convincing speech. I believe it is unanswerable. I w.a;s not incommoded

by tlie man wtho came into any riding and ispoke in favour of free agricultural implements, because I am in favour of free agricultural implements myself-as I am in favour of free everything else-But what greater credit could come to a young and ambitious member of parliament than to take up a case like that and prove it? Is not that his high duty and function as a member of parliament? What are these ministers going to do to earn their salaries when they get all these commissions appointed? Probably the most soholary and (best informed individual Tory I have met in this country said to me: I do not see what responsible government is coming to; what are we doing, making all these commissions? I agreed most emphatically with what he said. It is nothing less than an infraction of the principles of responsible government- You are handing over your duties, as we are handing over our responsibilities, to a commission. We have the word of the Minister of Finance that he would in every case give very great weight to what the commissioners said. And why not? If you pay men anything from $5,000 to $7,500, they ought to have some weight,-they certainly get some weight. They are to be an advisory board. If they give you advice and you take it they fix your faxes. If they give you .advice and you do not take it, you take back to the government -and to' parliament the -responsibilities of which -you have divested you-rs-elf and which you have given over to the commission. Th-ere -is no getting -away from the dilemma.
I was surprised to hear my right hon friend the Prime Minister compare his commission to a court. The -highest court in any British country is the high court of parliament itself; and when you make a smaller court-call it -a commission or what you may-and give it the duty that parliament has performed -within the British Empire from time immemorial, you Reduce the dignity and effectiveness of parliament and make it very likely that the status of a ^member of parliament and a member of the government will be lowered. P-arliament has been called not only 'the high court of parliament' but also the 'high inquest of the nation'-the high inquiring place, inquiring by the operations of their own minds. That is how they have earned the distinction that has crowned English_ statesmen in all generations, and that is how we have built up the greatest parliamentary institutions the world has ever seen.
Something has been said of the cost of production. My view is that there is a thing which a member of parliament has no right to talk about. For my part, I would begin to discuss the tariff at a much earlier point. And, personally, I do not
want any one to tell me about the cost of production on my farm; that is my business-; and, under freedom, I would run it and compete with the world. Talk about the defence of interests by acts ef government-I wish men on this side of the Atlantic would study, more than they find time to do in these busy days, the works of some of the biggest anen. Ralph Waldo ^ Emerson, than whom no prose writer is more worthy of our attention, dealing with this very argument, said: If you want to make men do not protect them by the shabby artifices of cunning tariffs; let their work defend them, let their works speak for thefrn. That is the 'cost of production' that I would like Canadians to go into.
I have tried to say a few words upon the principle of this Bill. I believe that it is emphatic-ally a new and a wrong departure. We have heard something about it being borrowed from the United States, and borrowed from Germany. I can conceive of no smaller r61e for Canada than borrowing the discarded ideas of any country, and in borrowing higher protection to-day, not even the member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) can say that he is likely to be borrowing very long from Germany. In Germany has happened an election only less in its consequence than that which happened when the repeal of the corn laws was carried in Britain. For the remarkable thing about these German elections is that the universal opinion of the population in the cities of that country that have returned Socialists is in favour of free trade. Their victories have been won even at the seat of royalty itself, there are 4,400,000 men, every one of them pledged to free trade, and thank God, also pledged to a reduction of armaments. We have had a scare on the question of armaments, which I do not think is affecting Canada so much now. But I am afraid that on this question of a Tariff Commission we have a scare with much more reality in it, but I shall only be too pleased if I happen to be wrong.

The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) opened with a statement that I had rather offended him in what I said in January, 1911. I was not only surprised but I was quite unable to conceive anything that I said that could have given rise to that conviction in his mind. However, it appears that the word ' exotic ' was not congenial to my hon friend.
It was very flattering. It means a rich, rare and tropical plant.

It is still more difficult to understand the offence that my hon. friend took from the word as it now appears

to him. There is no one less desirous of wounding the feelings of the hon. member for Red Deer than myself. Since the days that he entered the House I do not think that he has had a more attentive listener to his remarks than the humble member for Portage la Prairie. I have often marvelled, at and indeed I have studied to acer-tain the secret, of that most unusual power by which he is able to make what appeals, when read in ' Hansard,' as a very unconvincing speech when heard in the House itself spoken from his lips, most impressive. The term which I used of course strictly in the sense in which I understood it, that is to say as representing one born in another clime of thought, if I may so speak, and on another soil who has not yet reached in this country the stage where conditions are as familiar to him and as conducive to sane opinion as were the conditions in the old land. That was the sense in which I used it. My recollection of the word hovers around a very illustrious statesman, I think Robert Lowe, who first used that word in the English parliament, and Mr. Lowe, as the member for Red Deer will remember, was one of the most talented debaters that ever sat in the British House of Commons. In introducing this word he applied it to no less a distinguished institution than the established Church of England, and referred to it as an exotic plant on Irish soil. So the hon. member for Red Deer must realize that when I used the word in January, 1911, it was far from being intended in an offensive sense, because I have every respect for his opinions, as I have for the opinions of every other member of this House. The hon. member seems to think that I harbour some opinions .antagonistic to English immigration. How could he take such an inference from anything I said? I am sure that we welcome in this country every Englishman, no matter how rabid a free trader he may be. When I study history, I find that the right hon. leader, whom the member for Red Deer so humbly, and at one time so servilely followed, only fifteen years ago, preached doctrines now firmly believed in by the member for Red Deer; an.! when I reflect how far he has advanced since coming into closer contact with conditions in Canada, I may hope that in the course of fifteen years longer he (the hon. member for Red Deer) will even become qualified for a Conservative administration. The member for Red Deer also regretted that he did not have an opportunity of replying to my remarks last January. Now it is quite true that the motion'w,as moved on Wednesday, hut the member for Red Deer well knows that on three subsequent occasions it was reached on the order paiper, and on each occasion the right hon. leader of the opposition, Mr. MEIGITEN.
then leading the government, moved the adjournment of the House. I think on two of those occasions, I myself, rose and protested, and urged that the right hon. gentleman should permit a further discussion of this question, hut every one was silent on the government side, and no one was more silent than the member for Red Deer himself.

Before this clause passes, I would like to say a word or two. I am opposed to this Bill for the particular reason that it is asked for, and is in the interest of oniy one class in the country. Outside of the manufacturers, no class of people have asked for a Tariff Commission. There is no class of people outside the manufacturers who can benefit by this Tariff Commission. This Tariff Commission is to be appointed by the government for only one purpose, there is only _ one purpose that it can serve, and that is to advance the interests of the manufacturers of Canada. The Manufacturers' Association time and again, year after year, have asked that this commission should be appointed. Now, if it were simply for the purpose of getting statistics and information, the Minister of Finance has had a good business experience, and he could very well, with the officials in his own department, procure all the information that lie needs. If it was necessary to appoint more officials, he could do so; but- he would have officials who wouid be more likely to be non-partisan than any men who will be appointed by this government.
I think that if my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, was himself naming these commissioners they would be fairly well selected, but the Minister of Finance, if he will allow me to say so, is still somewhat young and innocent in political life, and I am afraid tihat it will not be only his voice that will carry weight, but that it will be the voice of the older sinners in that respect, who will want to make this commission an instrument for the purpose of helping out the manufacturers. Why is the government so ready to fulfil at once this particular promise that the Prime Minister made when he was touring the west? He made several other promises just as emphatically; as he made the promise to appoint a Tariff Commission. We have not heard of any steps on the part of the right hon. gentleman or his government to carry out and fulfil those promises because some of those promises were in response to the demands and applications of the farmers of Canada. This particular one was made in response to the demand and application of the manufacturers of Canada and nobody else. The Minister of Finance acknowledged last Wednesday, when he introduced the Bill that in so far as he knew there had been no demand from anyone

else outside the manufacturers to have this commission appointed.
The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain), a few moments ago, referred to wnat protection has done for the farmers. I can tell him what protection is doing for the farmers at the present time in my part of the country. Protection has done this for the farmers, that they have from 50,000 to 500,000 bushels of wheat lying in tthe open, the way you would pile broken stone to make a macadamized road, simply because the elevators are filled up with wheat, and the railways are paralyzed, and cannot supply cars; whereas, if the farmer were in absolutely the same position as the manufacturer he would have a market for his wheat, roads to carry it to market, and he would not be losing that wheat. We who represent agricultural constituencies are naturally afraid of what the effect of this Bill will be, it being a Bill absolutely in the interest of the manufacturers.
Will my hon friend explain to the House wherein the farmer differs from the manufacturer?
In.what regard?
My hon. friend was pointing out that, the manufacturer had a better opportunity than the farmer to ship his product. Will my hon. friend explain that?

The manufacturer is not limited in his market. The manufacturer getsi his raw material free of duty, but the farmer has his raw material taxed by the manufacturer, and does not get it free of duty. In that respect he is at a disadvantage.
The manufacturer doe- not sell his raw material, and if he wishes to send his manufactured goods to the United States he has to meet their tariff the same .as the farmer has to meet their tariff.

My hon. friend can twist around it as much as he likes, but the fact remains that the farmer lias been asking for a market for his product. The manufacturer is not asking for a market for Ins product outside; lie is asking to have the farmer hampered by keeping the duties up so that he will get the market at home. How are you helping the manufacturer, particularly when you are paralysing the purchasing power of the farmer? Where is the purchasing power oJ the farmer who has 1,000, or 2,000, or 5,000. or 10,000, bushels of wheat lying out with the snow' and rain falling on it, and not allowed to send it to the market that is open to the wheat, to the market that wants the wheat and to the man who is willing to pay for the wheat, and who would send that money into Canada where it would go eventually 93

to the manufacturer, because it resolves itself into this, as pointed out by the hon. member for Red Deer, that all production ends in consumption? We are afraid of this Bill, because as the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine, (Mr. Ames), told us the other day, the whole tendency of this government, with its well defined protective policy, is to increase protection. My hon. friend from Montreal, Si. Antoine, shakes his head. What about the duties now being levied, and the taxes collected on the lumber the farmer uses? What about the engines that are coming in, and that came in at a lower rate of duty a few months ago? They now come in at a higher rate of duty. There is one case in which they have taken the duty off altogether. Why? They took it off at the request of the manufacturers, because it was levied on an article that the manufacturer uses.	i
These are merely preventing iand correcting misapplications of the tariff.

Yes, preventing and putting on another interpretation, but ail in the interest of the manufacturers and against the interest of the farmers. That is why we are afraid of this Bill. Let us see what the manufacturers have been doing for a little while back. During the past three years there have been forty-one mergers; 190 individual companies were consolidated into these lorty-one mergers.
Is ti e grain growers merger for the purpose of speculating in wheat included in that number?

So far I have never heard of any grain growers merger. I have never heard of the grain growers merger, and if it were so the grain growers are not asking for protection to help them but they are asking for free trade. The main growers have not issued millions and millions of dollars of watered stock on which they want to collect from the consumers of Canada, 6, 7, or 8 per cent

stock that is not represented by one dollar of investment; yet that is what the manufacturers are doing and that is what this Bill is going to help them to do. These forty-one amalgamations represent a capitalization of $334,938,266, or almost $350,000,000. Let us see how that works out. T will take one or two individual instances. 1 will take the first on the list and I am quoting now from the 'Monetary Times.' I find first on the list Amalgamated Asbestos, which is a merger that took stock in six ether companies with a total capital-zat-ion of $3,550,000 and I know, as a matter of fact, that of that $3,550,000 a large amount was watered. What was the new capitalization?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What are the bonds selling for to-day?
That was before the 21st September, was it not??

If my hon. friends will just keep quiet for a moment they will get all the information they want. This amalgamation has a capitalization of twenty-five million dollars'; and, for the three -and-a-half million dollars the capitalization of the companies they took in, they issued eight million dollars worth of bonds, one million eight hundred and seventy-five thousand dollars preferred stock, and eight million one hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars common stock. The object of that amalgamation was to enable the mien who got the common stock for nothing, to collect dividends from the consumers on that common stock. That particular company has been a failure, as naturally they should, because they went a good deal too far and the bonds are selling at a very low figure to-day, and, so far as I know, the common stock and the preferred stock are worth nothing at all. Now, let us take the Ames-Holden-McCready, Limited, Montreal. That amalgamation took in the Ames-Holden Company with a capitalization of $2,500,000, and the James McCready Company, Limited, with a capitalization o-f $1,000,000, a total of $3,500,000. They capitalized that at $11,500,000, but they did not issue all that. They issued in bonds $1,000,000 and in preference stock $2,500,000, which covered exactly the capitalization of the two companies amalgamated. Then, they issued three million five hundred thousand dollars of common stock, all watered stock, not one dollar of value in it so far as anybody knows. And, this legislation that we are passing to-day is for the purpose of helping -such amalgamations as 1 have mentioned to take out of the farmers and the consumers of Canada interest on that common stock that has been issued.

As the name -of a company I have a connection with has been mentioned, may I say one word to the hon. member? I would like to say this: th^t if, upon investigation, it should be discovered by the Tariff Commission that the merger to which the hon. gentleman refers has in the slightest degree enhanced the -selling price of the articles to the consumer, I shall be most willing to consent that the thirty per cent duty which the Liberals put on boots and shoes should be reduced to twenty-five per cent, as it w-as under the Conservative government.

And so, the hon. member (Mr. Ame-s) excu-ses the whole thing on the ground that up to the present this amalgamation has not increased the cost of Mr. TURRIFF.
boots and -shoes. That is a statement that I accept from him, but I have heard dozens and scores of people within the last year or so complain of the -advanced price of boms and shoes. I am to-Cray wearing boots -exactly the same as I have worn for years -and I am now paying $1.00 a pair more than I paid for the -same boots a few years ago. They -are not made by the firm with which the hon. -member is connected, but by others. You can go into any store in Ottawa to-day and price boots and shoes and I venture the assertion that tlie-v are twenty per cent or twenty-five per cent higher than they were two or three years ago.
We should be delighted to have the Tariff Commission investigate the cost.
That is exactly what the hon. gentleman wants; he wants a Tariff Commission, and he wants to name the commissioners, and there is the whole trouble.
And if the government should change in the meantime, we would not drop the investigation on that account.

I want to point out to the Minister of Finance that I'do not care how honestly he may try he will not be able in the highly protected company he sits in at the council to get a commission that is not more or less- partisan, and this commission is for the purpose of reporting and ascertaining whether these manufacturers such as I have mentioned, and hundreds of others ought to be entitled to get protection enough to enable them to pay a dividend on common stock which is really watered stock. A year ago when the cement merger business came up, what was the argument of these gentlemen? It was, that they were entitled to get dividends on their money. What was the argument in connection with the bounty on steel? Not long ago I was in Alon-treal and a friend of mine who bought some of that common -stock was complaining. Some twenty million dollars of common stock was issued and never one dollar of it went into the treasury of the company, but the innocent purchaser of that stock to-day says; Why should I not get paid interest on that stock.
Does the hon. gentleman say that no cash was paid into the treasury of the Dominion Steel Company for that common stock?

That is what I said, and I got circulars from the Dominion Iron and Steel Company's brokers offering the preference stock at $85, and $100 of common stock t-hrowm in as a bonus, and it was advertised all over the Dominion.
I may state for the information of the hon. gentleman that a certain part of the issued common stock was paid for in cash; at least five million dollars was paid for.

Will the hon. member deny my statement that I was offered preference stock at $85 with one share of common stock thrown in as a bonus, for nothing. I know that statement is correct because I had the document in my hands making the offer and it was sent to me by mail.

I do not know what offers you may have received, but the preference shares were offered for subscription at $85 without any common stock bonus. I am sure the hon. member for Assiniboia is entirely mistaken in his statement regarding the preference tstock. I would say further that part of the Dominion Steel Company's issued common stock was paid for in cash, $5,000,000 at a substantial price.
May I ask the hon. member what the five million dollars' worth of common stock he has referred to was sold at?
About 60 1 think.
My information is that it was sold at 15.
That may be some additional cash which went into the treasury of the company.

Well, I do not care what the particulars are in any one particular case, but I do say that the whole tendency of these mergers is to put out millions and hundreds of millions of dollars worth of common stock, just exactly as in the case of the two companies I have men tioned, and the consumers and the farmers of Canada are expected to pay enhanced prices in order to pay dividends on that common stock which does not represent one dollar in the treasury, and that is all watered practically and should never have been issued. And, the intention of this legislation is to help the manufacturers by having a commission that will be favourable to them. That is what they are asking for. They are asking for a commission to get this information for the Minister of Finance. We all know that if you send out two or three different persons to collect information and make a report they will each differ as to the facts and possibly present reports from their own point of view, but when you have a commission working, as my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) stated, for a government that has' well known protective principles, you will have their report and the evidence, and the manner of 93*
taking the evidence, all with protectionist ideas and leaning towards higher protection.
So far as I can judge from the Bill, they will take the evidence that suits them, any that does not suit them, they do not need to record, and any evidence they take that does not suit the government, the Minister of Finance can place before the House or not, as he likes. There is nothing in this Bill to state that all information and ail findings of the commission will be laid before parliament for the use of the members and of the people of Canada.
Let us see one or two more companies that have amalgamated. Let us take the Dominion Canners, Limited, of Hamilton, Ontario. That conupany absorbed a large number of canning and preserving companies in Ontario. These companies had a total capitalization of $1,574,000. The companies were merged into the Dominion Canners, Limited, of Hamilton, Ontario, with a capitalization of $12,500,000, and for the $1,574,000 of combined capital of all those companies the Dominion Canners issued $1,500,000 in bonds,, $2,100,000 in preferred stock, and $2,100,000 of common stock. The balance of all this stock is in the treasury and it is to their interest, to the interest of the men who were in all these mergers, to have this Tariff Commission, and they are the men who have demanded it from the government, they are the men who want it, who will benefit by it. Nobody else wants it, nobody else has asked for it, and nobody else will benefit by it. The government is, I presume, carrying out pre-election pledges to these people, they are now delivering their part of the bargain.
Would it not be to the interest of the consumer to have a statement of what these men are taking out of the consumer? That is the object of the commission.

Yes, and the Customs Act provides that a judge of one of the High Courts should investigate that, but this Bill takes it out of the hands of the judge, and puts it into the hands of partisans appointed by the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) and his friends.
How many investigations were there into combines since the introduction of the Act?

The Minister of Labour will have all of that information in his department. The paper companies were investigated by a judge and the duties wera reduced in consequence. So my hon. friend will see how much better it has been to leave that part of it as it is, to leave the investigations in the hands of an independent judge, instead of men

[DOT]who may, or may not, be partisans, but who are much more likely to be than not.
Then there is the Matthews-Laing Company. This is an amalgamation of the '-George Matthews Company with a capital [DOT]of $1,000,000; the Park Blackwell Company [DOT]with a Capital of $500,000; and the Laing Packing and Provision Company, Limited, [DOT]with a capital of $500,000, a total of $2,000,-*000. This company has been formed with a capital of $7,000,000 and they have issued in bonds $1,200,000, in preferred stock, $2,000,000 and in common stock, $1,250,000. You cannot buy a dollar of the common stock on the market unless you buy some of the preferred stock or bonds as well. If you buy the preferred stock they will give you a bonus of common stock and allow you to buy a further proportion of common stock but they will not sell one [DOT]dollar's worth of common stock to a man who is not prepared to buy the preferred stock as well, showing that they expect, although they have capitalized at almost twice the capital of the companies that formed the merger, that the common stock will become very valuable. Will any one say that that has not had an effect on the price of meats? Any one in Ottawa will tell you what has taken i-uace in the last few months in reference to the cost of meat and other products controlled by these men.
These are the men from whom the commission will get information; they will give any information they please to the minister and the minister will give any information he pleases to the House. If the leader of ihe government had been as ready to carry out other promises he made prior to the election, his course would have been much better received throughout Canada because in all parts of the Dominion you have consumers, but you have not always manufacturers. My bon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) pointed out that, the manufacturers had put their money into these concerns. Will any one say that the farmer has not put his money into his business, and for every dollar engaged in manufacturing interests, how many hundreds are engaged in agriculture? I am not prepared to say what the proportion is, but I know there is a great deal more invested in agricultural pursuits than in manufacturing.
My point was that we should have protected the farmer as well.
But the manufacturer is asking for this commission and he gets it, and the farmer has asked to have the protection taken off and he cannot get it.
When?
They asked for free trade in natural products of the farm.
Oh, oh.

Yes, take the requests made by all agricultural societies throughout the Dominion of Canada, and they are practically all on the lines of getting free trade in natural products. Take the request made by all agricultural societies throughout the Dominion, and they are all practically in favour of free trade in natural products.
No.
Well, the great majority of them anyway.
Paid agitators.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) chooses to call the 700 or 800 farmers who appeared in this Commons chamber a year or two ago paid agitators, he may do so and let him take their judgment on what he says. They were not paid agitators-not one quarter of, or one tenth as much as the men the Manufacturers' Association sent around to get their ideas put into force. The manufacturers are the men who have the money to hire agitators.
Did not that large delegation of representative farmers ask the late government to remove the duty on agricultural implements, and did the late government do it?

They asked to have the duty taken off agricultural implements and they also asked to have reciprocity in farm products with the United States, also to have the British preference increased and a general reduction in the duties. Is my hon. friend, who interrupted me, prepared to give them what they ask?
Did the late government acquiesce in their request for a reduction or abolition of the duties on farm implements?

The farmers did ask foi a reduction on agricultural implements, and my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who was then leading the government introduced a measure reducing the duty on agricultural implements but it was defeated by hon. gentlemen opposite.
How much?
It was in my judgment not sufficient but more than the farmers are likely to get from the present government.

Is it not true that the late government reduced the duty 24 per cent? And is it not also true that official valuation of binders coming to this country prior to that was $80 each ard that subsequently that was raised to $100, so

293S
that the farmer paid more duty than he did before?

My hon. friend from Vancouver shows that he does not know much about farming and agricultural implements. In the one case he is speaking about the duty on a six foot binder and in the other on an tight foot binder. The resolution before the House is not in the interests of the farmer and as a representative of the agricultural interests I am opposed to it.

I have been somewhat amused, in common with other members, at the lectures we have been receiving from the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Turriff). He has produced no facts on which to ground his arguments. He has dealt entirely with suspicions and inuendoes in which he has considerable experience, and in this connection he reminds me of what took place some years ago when he was an official of the then government of the day. At that time he had something to do with the opening of tenders, and on a certain occasion-I cite this to show the suspicion which certain persons who were tenderers entertained of the good faith of the hon. gentleman- a certain gentleman from Simcoe, or some part of Ontario, who had submitted a tender for certain timber lands insisted, so strongly did he suspect the good faith of the hon. gentleman, on being present when the tenders were opened. This hon. gentleman, who now poses as such a staunch friend of the farmers, reminds me of a certain individual who for many years bad been engaged in the liquor traffic and had made a iarge fortune in selling liquor, and who, after he had acquired his fortune, became a very strong temperance advocate, but he took good care, while insisting on the necessity of prohibition, to hang on to the fortune he had acquired in the liquor traffic. The hon. gentleman reminds me very much of that temperance advocate in the state of Massachusetts.

As my hon. friend has referred to me while I was an official of the Department of the Interior, I may be allowed a moment to reply. My hon. friend and others who were then in the Cabinet, were very ready to make insinuations and cast suspicions, but when an investigation was called there was not one of them who had the courage to summon me as a witness, although I was waiting at the door day after day, demanding to be called, and give evidence. If my hon. friend wishes to revive any of these old matters he is at perfect liberty to do so. My hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) was equally free with his insinuations. He went out to my constituency with his magic lanterns
and insinuations, and at every place where be held meetings I doubled my majority.
It knocked out some of you all the same.

I noticed at the next session of parliament that my hon. friend -never opened his mouth in the House, he was in such bad odour with his own party.
If the hon. gentleman wants to go over that ground again, well and good. Let .him come out again with his insinuations and his magic lantern and my majority will be still further increased. I repeat that if any man wants to make any charge against me in connection with the opening of tenders, or the handling of Crown timber lands in the northwest, or anything else in connection with my official career, I shall be most happy to meet him and prove him a falsifier and his charges as lies.

If the hon. gentleman was not called as a witness before the investigation to which he has referred, it was no doubt out of kindness to him, because the committee knew the kind of evidence he was prepared to give, and did not want to hear him.
Progress reported.

I had intended moving the House into Committee of Supply. There are two resolutions in the Department of Public Works, and I wish to complete the work of this department so as to open the door for another department to take up its estimates to-morrow.

I think we ought to adjourn now. The time has come,
when we ought to adjourn.
If the House is not disposed to pass these two resolutions-

I do not know
whether it is so disposed or not.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk) will remember that the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) specially wanted the resolutions to stand as he had something to say about them. He is not here-
They stood at his request.
Yes, and naturally he would not expect that they would come up at this time of night.
I move the adjournment of the House.
Will we take up this same discussion to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.25 p.m.
Tuesday, February 13, 1912.
